# Data Center Water Use Tracker

> Tracking data center water consumption in Virginia & Ohio via public regulatory data (EPA ECHO DMR flow at receiving wastewater treatment plants, state permit portals, utility financial reports), plus curated national datasets: data-center water legislation, federal water-law cases relevant to data centers (CWA, SDWA, TSCA, RCRA, Rivers & Harbors Act) with a statutory-readings mapping, data-center sites with documented water conflicts, and company water claims.

Static build 2026-07-26. Dashboard: https://pranava0x0.github.io/datacenterwaterusage/ · Source: https://github.com/pranava0x0/datacenterwaterusage

## Key numbers

- 67 bills tracked — 22 Enacted · 33 Introduced · 12 Failed / Vetoed
- 107 federal water enforcement cases (CWA, SDWA, TSCA, RCRA, RHA) — 21 Data Center · 16 Data-Center Adjacent · 39 Industrial Water · 31 Landmark Precedent
- Core finding: data centers rarely hold their own discharge permits; operational water shows up at the receiving municipal treatment plant, so the pipeline tracks WWTP NPDES permits via EPA ECHO.

## Key principles across tracked legislation

- **Disclosure** (29 bills, 7 enacted): Require operators or utilities to file specific consumption reports. Examples: VA HB 496 / SB 553, TX SB 6, OR HB 3546.
- **Transparency** (29 bills, 7 enacted): Make data-center water/energy use publicly visible instead of proprietary. Examples: VA HB 496 / SB 553, UT HB 76, WV HB 4983.
- **Permit oversight** (24 bills, 10 enacted): Give regulators or localities approval leverage over siting and use. Examples: VA HB 496 / SB 553, TX SB 6, Loudoun County ZOAM 2025.
- **Cost allocation** (23 bills, 6 enacted): Make data centers pay the infrastructure and rate costs they cause. Examples: MN HF 16, TX SB 6, OR HB 3546.
- **Conservation** (19 bills, 7 enacted): Mandate or incentivize lower water/energy consumption outright. Examples: MN HF 16, OR HB 3546, ID H 895.
- **Preemptive review** (17 bills, 7 enacted): Force evaluation of impacts before construction, not after. Examples: MN HF 16, Loudoun County ZOAM 2025, Denver CB 26-0431.
- **Moratorium** (10 bills, 6 enacted): Pause new data-center development until safeguards exist. Examples: Denver CB 26-0431, NY EO 62, Prince George's County MD CB-2026 data center moratorium.
- **Federal coordination** (9 bills, 1 enacted): Standardize metrics and oversight across states at the federal level. Examples: US EO 14318, CA AB 1577, US HR 6984.
- **Best-practice guidance** (8 bills, 1 enacted): Codify model standards and guidance rather than hard mandates. Examples: Loudoun County ZOAM 2025, US HR 5332, IL SB 4016 / HB 5513.
- **Anti-corporate-welfare** (7 bills): Condition or repeal subsidies and tax exemptions. Examples: SC H 4583, NC HB 1063, AL SB 270.
- **Closed-loop cooling** (7 bills, 2 enacted): Require sealed cooling systems with minimal net water draw. Examples: MN HF 16, ID H 895, SC H 4583.
- **NDA prohibition** (5 bills): Ban the non-disclosure agreements that hide water deals from the public. Examples: OH HB 784, IL SB 4016 / HB 5513, US HR 8488.
- **Permitting acceleration** (3 bills, 3 enacted): Speed water permitting up for data centers, not slow it down. Examples: US EO 14318, US AI Action Plan 2025, QTS Richmond Technology Park DC5 (FAST-41).
- **Strict liability** (3 bills): Attach direct, non-waivable liability for violations or harms. Examples: SC H 4583, US HR 8488, KS SB 400.

## Legislation tracker

- FL SB 484 (Florida) — Enacted — Bars utilities from passing large-scale data-center electricity and infrastructure costs onto residential/small-business ratepayers and requires 50+ MW users to pay their full cost of service; requires data centers using at least 100,000 gallons/day to use reclaimed water for cooling when environmentally, economically, and technically feasible; requires public discussion of water/utility impacts before approval and preserves local governments' zoning/denial authority; tightens aquifer withdrawal permitting. Source: https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/484/ByCategory
- ID H 895 (Idaho) — Enacted — Requires data centers built after July 1, 2026 to design cooling systems for non-consumptive water use or to draw from a municipal/water-district system, and requires the Department of Water Resources director to issue findings when evaluating new water appropriations or transfers for data centers. Aimed at preserving groundwater for agriculture in Idaho's high desert. Source: https://legislature.idaho.gov/sessioninfo/2026/legislation/H0895/
- Denver CB 26-0431 (Local (Denver, CO)) — Enacted — Pauses acceptance and processing of new zoning permits and site development plans for data centers in the City and County of Denver for one year while the city drafts rules on water consumption, energy use, noise, and siting — adopted amid Denver Water's call for a 20% drought reduction and a proposed CoreSite facility estimated at ~235,000 gallons/day. Source: https://denver.legistar.com/View.ashx?M=F&ID=15376337&GUID=9AA8B5A2-CEC8-43E5-8752-C8EC3757EDBB
- Loudoun County ZOAM 2025 (Local (Loudoun County, Virginia)) — Enacted — Comprehensive zoning ordinance amendment removing by-right (administrative) approval pathway for data centers in Loudoun County. Now requires Special Exception (SPEX) approval with stringent legislative review and public hearings before Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors. Phase 2 (expected late 2026) will further tighten compatibility, water, and noise standards. Source: https://www.loudoun.gov/5990/Data-Center-Standards-Locations
- MD HB 270 / SB 116 (Maryland) — Enacted — Commissions a state study of the environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development: the Dept. of the Environment assesses effects on air and water quality and Chesapeake Bay restoration, the Maryland Energy Administration assesses energy demand and infrastructure, and the University of Maryland School of Business covers economic impacts. The report is due to the Governor and General Assembly by Sept. 1, 2026. Source: https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Legislation/Details/SB0116?ys=2025RS
- MN HF 16 (Minnesota) — Enacted — Water-appropriation permit process and DNR preapplication review for data centers expected to use >100M gal/yr; evaluates water source and conservation. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/94/2025/1/HF/16/
- NY EO 62 (New York) — Enacted — One-year pause on DEC discretionary permits for data centers at or above 50 MW. Orders the Department of Public Service to report on data-center impacts including water use and water quality, and directs DEC to assess within 12 months whether the state's water-withdrawal program needs new rules for very large users. Source: https://www.governor.ny.gov/executive-order/no-62-establishing-temporary-moratorium-data-centers-new-york-while-state-develops
- OR HB 3546 (Oregon) — Enacted — Creates a new utility customer classification for data centers, cryptocurrency operations, and other large industrial energy users (>20 MW). Requires them to pay their full share of electricity costs and transmission upgrades and to sign 10-year minimum-commitment contracts. Source: https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2025R1/Measures/Overview/HB3546
- Prince George's County MD CB-2026 data center moratorium (Prince George's County, Maryland) — Enacted — A two-year pause on hyperscale data-center development — the longest in Maryland — adopted with unanswered questions about the facilities' effect on county water among the stated reasons. Source: https://marylandmatters.org/2026/07/08/prince-georges-county-extends-pause-on-hyperscale-data-center-development/
- Santa Fe County NM data center moratorium (Santa Fe County, New Mexico) — Enacted — An 18-month pause adopted unanimously, extended from the 12 months originally proposed, with the regulatory threshold lowered from 100 MW to 1 MW — by far the lowest trigger of any tracked moratorium. Source: https://www.santafecountynm.gov/news/detail/santa-fe-county-approves-18-month-moratorium-on-data-centers
- SD SB 135 (South Dakota) — Enacted — Data centers with peak electrical demand of 10 MW or greater must cover the electrical-infrastructure costs they cause (including stranded costs if they leave) and must coordinate with water service providers so their water use stays within locally approved supply; the state may not preempt local ordinances regulating data centers. Source: https://legiscan.com/SD/bill/SB135/2026
- TX SB 6 (Texas) — Enacted — Imposes new planning, interconnection, and cost-recovery rules on large electric loads (≥75 MW) in ERCOT, including data centers. Requires backup-generation disclosure capable of meeting a share of site demand, mandates remote-disconnect capability for emergency load shedding, and forces disclosure of duplicative interconnection requests across utilities. Source: https://capitol.texas.gov/BillLookup/History.aspx?LegSess=89R&Bill=SB6
- US EO 14318 (United States) — Enacted — Directs the Army Corps to identify or develop a data-center-specific nationwide permit under CWA §404 and Rivers and Harbors Act §10, establishes NEPA categorical exclusions for data-center infrastructure, provides for programmatic ESA §7 consultation covering multi-year construction windows, and expands FAST-41 coverage to qualifying data centers. Sets the >100 MW 'Data Center Project' and $500M / national-security 'Qualifying Project' thresholds the implementing actions key off. Source: https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/accelerating-federal-permitting-of-data-center-infrastructure/
- US AI Action Plan 2025 (United States) — Enacted — The policy blueprint EO 14318 implements. Calls for a data-center-tailored Clean Water Act §404 nationwide permit, new NEPA categorical exclusions, FAST-41 expansion, and streamlining or reduction of Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act and CERCLA requirements for AI infrastructure. Source: https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf
- UT HB 76 (Utah) — Enacted — Large data centers (redefined as 10,000+ sq ft, down from 50,000) must notify water providers of their projected water demand and report their actual water consumption to the state. A committee substitute made the water data more publicly transparent after criticism that the original version would have shielded individual facilities' use from public records. Source: https://le.utah.gov/~2026/bills/static/HB0076.html
- UT EO 2026-03 (Utah) — Enacted — Directs all state agencies to weigh water use (specifically Great Salt Lake impacts), air quality, wildlife, utility ratepayer costs, and public transparency alongside economic growth when reviewing data center projects. Creates formal Data Center Framework for state agency review. Source: https://governor.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026.05.29-EO-Higher-Bar-for-Data-Center-Development-1.pdf
- VA HB 496 / SB 553 (Virginia) — Enacted — Water utilities must report the monthly volume of water delivered to data centers, including reclaimed water. Source: https://lis.virginia.gov/bill-details/20261/SB553
- VA DEQ waterworks data-center reporting regulations (Virginia) — Enacted — Requires waterworks operators to report monthly water sales categorized as data-center-with-air-permit, domestic, industrial-commercial, or other, each split potable vs non-potable. Individual facility figures remain trade-secret protected; the published data is aggregate. Source: https://www.whro.org/environment/2026-06-26/new-regulations-beef-up-data-centers-required-water-use-reporting-in-virginia
- QTS Richmond Technology Park DC5 (FAST-41) (Virginia) — Enacted — The first data center ever granted FAST-41 coverage, putting its federal environmental review on a published, coordinated schedule with the Army Corps as lead agency. Covers two additional buildings at an existing four-building Henrico County campus. Source: https://www.permitting.gov/newsroom/press-releases/first-data-center-project-gains-permitting-councils-fast-41-coverage
- Washington County MD data center moratorium (Washington County, Maryland) — Enacted — A one-year pause on data-center development in western Maryland, with farm wells and drought conditions among the stated rationales. Source: https://thedailyrecord.com/2026/07/01/washington-county-approves-yearlong-data-center-moratorium/
- WV HB 4983 (West Virginia) — Enacted — Authorizes a Dept. of Commerce legislative rule setting the certification process for 'high impact' data centers and microgrid districts (implementing 2025's HB 2014) and keeps key project details confidential. A Senate amendment added only soft language directing that potential water use be 'studied' and water sources given 'mindful protections'; floor amendments to require pre-operation water-impact assessments and to limit groundwater use were rejected. Source: https://www.wvlegislature.gov/Bill_Status/bills_text.cfm?billdoc=hb4983+intr.htm&yr=2026&sesstype=RS&i=4983
- York County SC data center moratorium (York County, South Carolina) — Enacted — A nine-month pause in unincorporated York County directing staff to examine groundwater, noise, utility rates, energy infrastructure, waste heat and impacts on neighbouring properties, and to recommend whether independent experts should be retained. Source: https://www.wrhi.com/2026/07/york-county-council-approves-nine-month-data-center-moratorium-214184
- AL SB 270 (Alabama) — Introduced — Directs the Alabama Public Service Commission to review utility contracts with large-scale data centers (≥150 MW) to ensure they provide for full recovery of incremental service costs and demonstrate 'positive benefits' for ratepayers statewide. Requires PSC findings before contracts take effect. Source: https://legiscan.com/AL/bill/SB270/2026
- CA AB 1577 (California) — Introduced — Requires data-center owners to report location, size, PUE, WUE, total water consumption, and on-site fuel use to the California Energy Commission; CEC publishes annual aggregated/anonymized data and adds a data-center electrical-load assessment to the 2029 IEPR. Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1577
- CA AB 2619 (California) — Introduced — Requires data center operators to disclose projected water use, source, and volumes to their water supplier before obtaining a business license; upon renewal, requires reporting of actual annual water consumption. Directs DWR and CEC to develop water efficiency best practices by Jan 1, 2029. Successor to vetoed CA AB 93 (2025). Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB2619
- CA SB 887 (California) — Introduced — Prohibits categorical CEQA exemptions for data center projects; creates expedited judicial review pathway for data centers meeting clean energy and water efficiency standards under the Environmental Leadership Development Project program. Companion to AB 2619. Source: https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb887
- US HR 6984 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Directs EPA and EIA to collect and publish data on data centers' electricity consumption and air- and water-quality impacts, with EIA reporting every six months. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6984
- US HR 5332 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Directs the Comptroller General to conduct a technology assessment of liquid-cooling systems for AI compute clusters and HPC facilities and to develop federal best-practice guidance for agencies; does NOT impose mandatory rules on private data centers. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/5332
- US S. 4213 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Would require data-center operators to report actual energy and water consumption (plus five-year pre-construction estimates) to their states; states would aggregate/anonymize data for EPA, DOE, and USDA, who would issue joint regional reports and could fine non-compliance. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/4213
- US S. 4214 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Imposes a federal moratorium on construction of new AI data centers until safeguards are enacted ensuring the facilities do not increase utility bills, exacerbate climate impacts, deny community veto authority, or undermine labor standards. Also bans export of US AI computing infrastructure to countries without environmental, labor, and safety safeguards. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/4214
- US S. 3682 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Directs FERC to require grid operators to establish 'data center load queues' allowing utilities to prioritize or delay DC interconnections based on grid reliability and affordability. Encourages every state with at least one DC to establish DC-specific rate classes ensuring DC owners bear the full cost of generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades they trigger. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3682
- US HR 7066 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Updates federal utility cost-allocation policy under PURPA so that large electricity users like data centers bear the costs of grid infrastructure they require, while incentivizing zero-emission electricity sourcing. Aims to prevent cost-shifting onto residential and small commercial ratepayers. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/7066
- US HR 8488 (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Requires AI data center developers to publicly disclose proposed sites at least 180 days before any definitive development step. Mandates community engagement, multilingual outreach, and disclosure of projected electricity use, water consumption, cooling demands, and environmental impacts. Restricts NDAs and treats violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act. Source: https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8488
- US S. — Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act (Durbin; number TBD) (Federal (US)) — Introduced — Would require data-center operators to report actual energy and water consumption (plus five-year pre-construction estimates) to their states; states would aggregate/anonymize data for EPA, DOE, and USDA, who would issue joint regional reports and could fine non-compliance. Source: https://www.durbin.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/as-utility-costs-rise-durbin-introduces-new-legislation-to-bring-transparency-to-energy-and-water-consumption-by-data-centers
- IL SB 4016 / HB 5513 (Illinois) — Introduced — Requires data centers to pay for their own energy infrastructure and invest in renewable generation, disclose annual water consumption (intake + discharge) to the Illinois DNR beginning Jan. 1, 2027, identify and monitor likely pollutants in discharges to WWTPs, ban NDAs between local governments and DC operators, and mandate transparent community-benefit agreements. Source: https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=4016&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&SessionID=114&GA=104
- IA HF 2690 (Iowa) — Introduced — Requires data centers to file quarterly water-use reports with the Iowa DNR (volume, source, and efficiency) and quarterly energy reports with the Iowa Utilities Commission, with the reported information posted publicly online within 30 days; also requires a separate electric tariff so data-center costs are not shifted onto other ratepayers. Source: https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/publications/LGI/91/HF2690.pdf
- MI SB 762 (Michigan) — Introduced — Requires the Michigan Public Service Commission to publish annual public reports of each data center's water usage (by service area) and electricity consumption (in GWh) beginning in 2027. Source: https://legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-SB-0762
- MI SB 1018-1020 (Michigan) — Introduced — Bipartisan package that would halt data center development until April 1, 2027, pending development of comprehensive water, energy, and environmental standards. Source: https://michiganadvance.com/2026/06/24/michigan-lawmakers-residents-renew-push-for-statewide-data-center-moratorium/
- MI SB 1046-1050 (Michigan) — Introduced — SB 1046 would require a permit for water users at or above 550,000 gallons per day, cap consumptive use at 2 MGD, mandate at least three pre-application public hearings, require annual reporting from 2027 and allow permit revocation for reporting failures. SB 1049 would bar non-disclosure agreements where tax incentives were received. SB 1050 would require community benefit agreements covering water. Source: https://www.multistate.us/insider/2026/7/15/michigan-data-center-legislation-targets-energy-use-and-community-benefits
- NJ S3379 (New Jersey) — Introduced — Requires data center owners/operators to submit semi-annual water and energy usage reports to the NJ Board of Public Utilities for three years. Reports must cover total kWh, IT-equipment energy, water input (cubic meters), and source. State-incentivized facilities must also report PUE, WUE, and renewable energy factor. BPU publishes facility data within 30 days; performance metrics released only in anonymized aggregated form (n≥5). Source: https://pub.njleg.gov/Bills/2026/S3500/3379_I1.HTM
- NY S6394 / A9086 (New York) — Introduced — Requires data centers ≥5 MW to file pre-construction disclosure reports with the PSC covering location, labor, projected energy/water usage, waste heat, and water pollution. Mandates annual sustainability updates. Sets a renewable-energy schedule: 33% by 2030, 67% by 2035, 100% by 2040. Prohibits utility fossil-fuel PPA incentives and directs PSC to create a DC surcharge funding low- and moderate-income energy assistance in host communities. Source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S6394
- NY S9144 / A10141 (New York) — Introduced — Imposes a moratorium of at least three years and ninety days on the issuance of permits for new private data centers ≥20 MW. Directs DEC to publish a generic environmental impact statement and PSC to issue orders minimizing rate impacts. Public-sector projects like the state's Empire AI research initiative are exempt. Source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9144
- NY S10642 / A11560 (New York) — Introduced — Imposes a one-year statewide moratorium on permits for hyperscale data centers (peak load over 20 MW), requires environmental impact reporting on water consumption, discharge, and local water-system impacts, mandates separate water and electricity rate classes for large data centers, and pushes measures such as closed-loop cooling to prevent wastewater-infrastructure strain. Source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S10642
- NY DPS Data Center Impact Report (EO 62) (New York) — Introduced — The proceeding EO 62 orders: a DPS report on data-center impacts with water use and water quality expressly in scope, running alongside DEC's assessment of whether the water-withdrawal permitting program needs large-user rules. Source: https://www.governor.ny.gov/executive-order/no-62-establishing-temporary-moratorium-data-centers-new-york-while-state-develops
- NC HB 1063 (North Carolina) — Introduced — Mandates that data centers publicly report electricity consumption, peak demand, water consumption, cooling systems, and emissions-free generation. Facilities using over 1 billion liters of water per year or peak demand >40 MW must source at least 25% of power from non-emitting generation. Repeals state sales/use tax exemption for DC construction and server replacement. Source: https://www.ncleg.gov/BillLookUp/2025/H1063
- OH SB 378 (Ohio) — Introduced — Makes data centers responsible for the water/sewer infrastructure costs they cause, requires a Division of Water Resources permit to consume water, and caps consumptive use at 5 MGD averaged over 30 days. Source: https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/136/sb378
- OH HB 784 (Ohio) — Introduced — Enacts ORC 9.484 / 1521.301: requires data centers withdrawing waters of the state to file monthly and annual water-consumption reports with the Division of Water Resources and bars data-center water info from NDAs with political subdivisions. Source: https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/136/hb784
- OH HB 706 (Ohio) — Introduced — Codifies the PUCO-approved AEP Ohio data center tariff statewide. Requires new DC customers ≥25 MW to commit to paying for a minimum of 85% of subscribed electricity usage for up to 12 years, regardless of actual consumption. Bars utilities from recovering DC-driven costs by shifting them to other classes of customers. Source: https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/legislation/136/hb706
- OH EPA OHD000001 (draft general permit) (Ohio) — Introduced — First-of-its-kind NPDES general permit covering data center wastewater and stormwater discharges to waters of the state. Eligible facilities could obtain coverage for non-contact cooling water, cooling tower blowdown, boiler blowdown, air compressor condensate, and industrial stormwater via Notice of Intent (NOI) rather than individual NPDES permits. Sets monitoring parameters: temperature, pH, TSS, oil and grease, phosphorus, residual chlorine/oxidants. Source: https://epa.ohio.gov/divisions-and-offices/surface-water/permitting/ohnpdes-general-permits
- PA HB 2246 (Pennsylvania) — Introduced — Requires data centers planning to use more than 100,000 gallons of water per day over any 30-day period to notify the PA Department of Environmental Protection before commencing construction. Authorizes DEP review of proposed withdrawals against watershed capacity. Source: https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2246
- PA HB 2150 (Pennsylvania) — Introduced — Establishes annual energy and water reporting requirements for data centers in PA. Requires PA DEP and PUC to jointly issue annual reports on the cumulative impacts of data center energy and water use across the Commonwealth. Source: https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2150
- SC H 4583 (South Carolina) — Introduced — Would require data centers to use closed-loop water/liquid cooling with zero net withdrawal and zero wastewater discharge, mandate annual third-party-verified certifications, and impose strict liability for environmental damage. Source: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/sess126_2025-2026/bills/4583.htm
- SC HB 4583 (South Carolina) — Introduced — Requires data centers to use closed-loop cooling systems resulting in zero net water withdrawal and net zero wastewater discharge; prohibits groundwater extraction or municipal water use for cooling. Source: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/sess126_2025-2026/bills/4583.htm
- TX PUC Energy and Water Use Survey (data centers) (Texas) — Introduced — A survey directed by the Legislature in the 2025 budget, collecting electricity and water use from data centers and virtual-currency mining facilities. The only water-specific utility-commission action found nationally — the marquee data-center rate dockets elsewhere (PUCO 24-508-EL-ATA, the Georgia PSC large-load tariff, Dominion's SCC proceedings) are energy-only and carry no water provisions. Source: https://www.puc.texas.gov/industry/water/utilities/energy-and-water-use-survey/faq/
- VA SB 417 (Virginia) — Introduced — Conditions eligibility for Cloud Computing Cluster Infrastructure Grant Fund awards on the data center using treated (reclaimed) wastewater rather than potable water in its cooling systems — an incentive-based approach rather than a cooling-technology mandate. Source: https://lis.virginia.gov/bill-details/20261/SB417
- CA AB 93 (California) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required data centers to disclose projected water use to their water supplier at business-license application and certify actual annual water use at license renewal. Source: https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab93
- CO SB26-102 (Colorado) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required operators of new large-load data centers to comply with operational water management requirements and to report annual electricity and water consumption to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (first reports due June 30, 2028). Killed in committee at the sponsor's request. Source: https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/SB26-102
- CT SB 245 (Connecticut) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have repealed Connecticut's data-center tax incentives (PA 21-1) and conditioned data centers on meeting the state's clean-electricity standard (100% clean by 2040), paying prevailing wage, and meeting a sustainable-design / green-building standard; framed by the committee around data centers' water and energy use. Source: https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/JFR/S/PDF/2026SB-00245-R00ET-JFR.PDF
- GA SB 421 (Georgia) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have barred Georgia local governments, authorities, and political subdivisions from entering NDAs concealing a data center's water or electricity usage. Source: https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/SB421/2025
- IL SB 3830 (POWER Act) (Illinois) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required data centers to source renewable energy, submit quarterly water use reports, and submit water management plans to the IL Water Survey. Included community benefits agreements and ratepayer protection provisions. Source: https://www.circleofblue.org/2026/water-policy-politics/illinois-fails-to-pass-landmark-act-requiring-responsible-data-center-energy-and-water-use/
- IN SB 79 (Indiana) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have created an Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission working group to forecast data-center electricity demand (report by Oct. 31, 2026), required operators to file quarterly electricity-use reports the IURC publishes online, and required local governments to obtain projected power and water-use disclosures plus a site assessment before issuing data-center permits. Source: https://iga.in.gov/legislative/2026/bills/senate/79
- IA HF 2447 (Iowa) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required data centers to file quarterly water-use reports (volume, source, efficiency) with Iowa DNR and quarterly energy reports with the Iowa Utilities Commission, with public posting within 30 days, and directed IUC to create a data-center-specific rate class. Source: https://www.legis.iowa.gov/legislation/BillBook?ba=HF2447&ga=91
- KS SB 400 (Kansas) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required data centers in Kansas to use closed-loop cooling systems and authorized municipalities, county/district attorneys, and the AG to seek injunctions against non-compliant facilities. Source: https://www.kslegislature.gov/b2025_26/bills/sb400/
- ME LD 307 (Maine) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have imposed a moratorium on municipal and state permitting of data centers with loads of 20 MW or more until November 1, 2027 while a new Data Center Coordination Council studied impacts including water and energy infrastructure demands. Vetoed by Gov. Mills, who said she would have signed it with an exemption for the Androscoggin Mill project in Jay that reuses existing water infrastructure. Source: http://www.mainelegislature.org/legis/bills/display_ps.asp?ld=307&PID=1456&snum=132
- WA HB 2515 (Washington) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required data center operators to file a sustainability report disclosing server-cooling technology and water/energy use and emissions, directed utilities to adopt a data-center cost-recovery tariff by 2027 so other ratepayers do not subsidize them, and required large loads to curtail electricity use during grid stress. Source: https://washingtonstatestandard.com/2026/03/02/its-lights-out-for-wa-legislatures-effort-to-regulate-data-centers/
- WV HB 4832 (West Virginia) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have designated data centers high-volume water users, required them to submit water quantity and quality impact analyses to DEP, mandated public notice and hearings before approval, and authorized DEP to prohibit or limit withdrawals where adverse impacts to a state water resource would occur. Source: https://www.wvlegislature.gov/Bill_Text_HTML/2026_SESSIONS/RS/bills/hb4832%20intr.pdf
- WI AB 840 / SB 843 (Wisconsin) — Failed / Vetoed — Would have required data centers to recycle the water used to cool computer equipment, report water usage to the Wisconsin DNR, and meet utility-rate requirements ensuring facilities, not residential ratepayers, pay for their energy and water infrastructure demands. Source: https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/2025/proposals/ab840

## Federal water-law toolkit (statutory readings)

- cwa-402-npdes — CWA §402 / 33 U.S.C. §1342 (with §301, 33 U.S.C. §1311) (NPDES permit for direct discharge): Applies whenever a data center discharges cooling-tower blowdown, on-site treatment effluent, or process water directly to surface water rather than to a sewer. The AWS Lake Anna VPDES draft permit is the first direct cooling-discharge NPDES action at a hyperscaler campus; the Homer City PA draft permit covers cooling outfalls at a DC power plant. Once a campus holds its own NPDES permit, every exceedance is ECHO-visible and enforceable — including by citizen suit. Example cases: Smithfield-Pagan-River-1997, AWS-LakeAnnaVA-VPDES-cooling-discharge-2026, HomerCity-IndianaCounty-PA-NPDES-2026, Hanover-Foods-2025, PortOfMorrow-DEQ-OR-2024.
- cwa-402-construction-stormwater — CWA §402 Construction General Permit (Construction stormwater (CGP)): The primary CWA touchpoint for data centers today: multi-hundred-acre campus build-outs generate sediment-laden runoff, and every documented DC stormwater enforcement (Google Stillwater OK, Microsoft Boydton VA, QTS Fayetteville GA, Johns Hopkins DSAI) arose here. Enforcement usually names the general contractor — the permittee — not the operator. Example cases: Google-Stillwater-OK-stormwater-2025, Microsoft-Boydton-VA-2023, QTS-Fayetteville-GA-2024, JohnsHopkins-DSAI-Baltimore-2025, Energix-VA-2024.
- cwa-402-industrial-stormwater — CWA §402 Multi-Sector General Permit (Industrial stormwater (MSGP)): Post-construction exposure for campuses with exposed fuel farms, chemical storage, switchyards, and equipment yards. Most operating data centers hold only this near-empty stormwater permit — which is why the operational record is thin — but benchmark exceedances are public and enforceable. Example cases: Google-Stillwater-OK-stormwater-2025.
- cwa-404-dredge-fill — CWA §404 / 33 U.S.C. §1344 (Dredge-and-fill of wetlands and streams): Site-grading at greenfield campuses regularly crosses wetlands and headwater streams: Google's three pending §404 individual permit applications (Project Raspberry and Loch in VA, Port of Little Rock AR at 16.8 acres), the SDC ATLA Douglas County GA application with ~1 mile of stream impacts, and the Amazon New Carlisle IN cease-work order all sit here. The 2026 NWP 39 reissuance expressly enumerates data centers. Example cases: Amazon-NewCarlisle-IN-wetlands-2025, Google-ProjectRaspberry-VA-2026, Google-LittleRock-AR-2026, SDC-ATLA-DouglasCounty-GA-404-401-2025, USACE-NWP39-DataCenters-2026, Sackett-v-EPA-2023.
- cwa-401-certification — CWA §401 / 33 U.S.C. §1341 (State water-quality certification): Every data-center §404 permit needs a companion §401 certification, so state agencies (and commenters in the state proceeding) get leverage even where federal jurisdiction survives Sackett only barely. The SDC ATLA GA matter pairs §404 with a contested §401; the 4th Circuit's WV vacatur shows certifications are litigable. Example cases: SierraClub-WVDEP-401-2023, SDC-ATLA-DouglasCounty-GA-404-401-2025, Amazon-NewCarlisle-IN-wetlands-2025.
- cwa-307-pretreatment — CWA §307(b) / 33 U.S.C. §1317 (40 C.F.R. Part 403) (Pretreatment — industrial users of sewers): The regime that most directly governs operating data centers: cooling-tower blowdown (concentrated dissolved solids, biocides, corrosion inhibitors) goes to the sewer under an industrial-user permit. High-volume DC loading can cause POTW pass-through — putting the plant in violation of its own NPDES permit, as at Port of Morrow OR. IU permits and local limits are FOIA-able. Example cases: Swift-Beef-Grand-Island-2011, Yuengling-Pottsville-2016, Reading-WWTP-2024, PortOfMorrow-DEQ-OR-2024, Agri-Star-Postville-IA-2024-2025.
- cwa-316-cooling — CWA §316(a)/(b) / 33 U.S.C. §1326 (Thermal discharge and cooling-water intake): Bites hardest where a campus takes surface water for once-through or evaporative cooling, or pairs with on-site generation — the full power-plant profile. The AWS Lake Anna draft permit and the Homer City DC power plant put §316 review squarely into data-center permitting for the first time. Example cases: Brayton-Point-Dominion-2003-2007, Entergy-v-Riverkeeper-2009, Greenidge-SenecaLake-NY-2025, AWS-LakeAnnaVA-VPDES-cooling-discharge-2026, HomerCity-IndianaCounty-PA-NPDES-2026.
- cwa-311-spills — CWA §311 / 33 U.S.C. §1321 (SPCC, 40 C.F.R. Part 112) (Oil and hazardous-substance spills; SPCC plans): Data centers keep multi-million-gallon diesel fuel farms for backup generators — squarely SPCC-regulated. A tank or transfer release reaching a stream is legally identical to the pipeline cases, including the duty-to-report trap. The Johns Hopkins DSAI matter already pairs construction stormwater with a §311 diesel element. Example cases: Plains-Pipeline-Santa-Barbara-2020, Norfolk-Southern-East-Palestine-2024, JohnsHopkins-DSAI-Baltimore-2025.
- cwa-303-wqs — CWA §303 / 33 U.S.C. §1313 (antidegradation, TMDLs) (Water-quality standards and antidegradation review): A procedural lever at the siting stage: a proposed new DC outfall into high-quality water must survive an alternatives analysis (e.g., closed-loop or dry cooling), and a discharge into a TMDL-capped watershed inherits tighter limits. Raised by commenters in the Lake Anna proceeding. Example cases: AWS-LakeAnnaVA-VPDES-cooling-discharge-2026.
- cwa-402-maui-groundwater — CWA §402 via County of Maui (2020) (‘Functional equivalent’ discharge through groundwater): Closes the loophole for campuses that dispose of blowdown or treated effluent via injection wells, drywells, rapid-infiltration basins, or land application near streams: if it reaches surface water, Maui says permit it. Fact-intensive (distance, travel time), but the most potent novel theory for inland campuses over shallow aquifers. Example cases: County-of-Maui-v-Hawaii-Wildlife-Fund-2020, Maui-remand-DHaw-2021.
- cwa-505-citizen-suit — CWA §505 / 33 U.S.C. §1365 (Citizen suits): The enforcement backstop when agencies stand down: DMR exceedances at a DC's own NPDES permit, at its contractor's CGP coverage, or at the receiving POTW are all citizen-suit predicates — and this tracker's ECHO SNC/DMR pull is exactly the evidence base a §505 notice letter needs. QTS Fayetteville and TransGas Adams Fork began as riverkeeper notices. Example cases: Atlanta-RMClayton-CRK-2024-2026, QTS-Fayetteville-GA-2024, TransGas-AdamsFork-WV-2025, PortOfTacoma-v-PugetSoundkeeper-9thCir-2024, CERF-v-Naples-9thCir-2024.
- sdwa-1431-emergency — SDWA §1431 / 42 U.S.C. §300i (Emergency powers — imminent endangerment of drinking water): The fastest federal hook if a data-center-linked contaminant (fuel release, cooling-chemistry constituents, construction-driven nitrate or sediment) shows up in wells or a public system's source water. The Amazon Boardman nitrate fact pattern — contaminated domestic wells near DC-hosting farmland — is exactly the §1431 profile, and EPA has pledged investigation of the Meta Newton County GA well complaints. Example cases: Flint-MI-SDWA-1431-2016, DuPont-WashingtonWorks-PFOA-2005-2009, Trinity-American-v-EPA-SDWA-1431-1998, Amazon-Boardman-OR-nitrate-2026, Meta-MorganCo-GA-investigation-2026.
- sdwa-uic-classv — SDWA Part C UIC / 42 U.S.C. §300h (40 C.F.R. Parts 144–147) (Underground Injection Control — Class V wells): Directly regulates common campus infrastructure: stormwater drywells and infiltration galleries, geothermal/aquifer-thermal cooling return wells, and any on-site disposal of treated effluent to the subsurface are Class V wells requiring inventory, rule authorization, or permits — an underused federal hook over inland campuses that never touch surface water. Example cases: EPA-UIC-ClassV-MotorVehicleWells-1999.
- sdwa-1424e-sole-source-aquifer — SDWA §1424(e) / 42 U.S.C. §300h-3(e) (Sole-source aquifer project review): Reaches data-center projects only through a federal-funding hook — federally backed loans, grants, or infrastructure assistance for a campus or its supporting utilities over a designated aquifer trigger EPA review. Relevant to Texas Hill Country and San Antonio-area siting over the Edwards, and to any federally financed AI-infrastructure build-out. Example cases: Edwards-Aquifer-SoleSource-Designation-1975.
- sdwa-pws-compliance — SDWA Part B / 42 U.S.C. §300g (national primary drinking water regulations) (Public water system regulation and enforcement): Two directions: (1) a large campus with its own wells serving hundreds of workers can itself become a regulated PWS; (2) the small municipal systems that serve mega-campuses take on PWS compliance risk when DC demand strains capacity or forces new sources — the Richland Parish LA and Bessemer AL supply fights are about systems absorbing that risk. Example cases: US-v-Alisal-Water-Corp-2005, Flint-MI-SDWA-1431-2016.
- sdwa-source-water-protection — SDWA §§1452–1453 (source water assessment); state wellhead protection (Source-water and wellhead protection): The mapping layer for siting fights: a campus, fuel farm, or drainfield inside a delineated source-water protection area gives residents and utilities a concrete, government-authored basis to object — the posture of the Occoquan Reservoir objections to the PW Digital Gateway and the aquifer-recharge zoning fights in Texas and Georgia. Example cases: Google-Berkeley-SC-Middendorf-aquifer-2019, CorpusChristi-SintonTX-EvangelineAquifer-wells-2026.
- tsca-8e-substantial-risk — TSCA §8(e) / 15 U.S.C. §2607(e) (Substantial-risk information reporting): Reaches the chemical suppliers behind data-center water chemistry — cooling-tower biocides, corrosion inhibitors, film-forming additives, and legacy AFFF fire suppressants. If a supplier or large processor learns its formulation is contaminating water near campuses and sits on it, that is the DuPont fact pattern. Example cases: DuPont-WashingtonWorks-PFOA-2005-2009, 3M-TSCA-8e-PFAS-2006.
- tsca-8a7-pfas-reporting — TSCA §8(a)(7) / 15 U.S.C. §2607(a)(7) (40 C.F.R. Part 705) (One-time PFAS manufacture/import reporting): Indirect but growing: imported electrical equipment, coolants (some immersion-cooling fluids are PFAS), and fire-suppression stocks can pull vendors into reporting, and the public dataset gives water advocates a way to trace PFAS found near a campus back to a supply chain as NPDES PFAS limits tighten (see the Chemours Washington Works effluent-limits consent agreement). Example cases: TSCA-PFAS-Reporting-Rule-2023, Chemours-Washington-Works-PFAS-2023.
- rcra-7002-7003-endangerment — RCRA §§7002–7003 / 42 U.S.C. §§6972(a)(1)(B), 6973 (Imminent-and-substantial-endangerment actions (solid waste → groundwater)): The gap-filler where Sackett cuts off CWA jurisdiction: contamination migrating through soil and groundwater from fuel releases, construction fill, sludge, or spent cooling-treatment chemicals at a campus can support a §7002(a)(1)(B) citizen suit even with no surface-water connection at all — the same post-Sackett role Maui plays for connected waters. Example cases: Interfaith-v-Honeywell-RCRA-2003-2005, Amazon-Boardman-OR-nitrate-2026.
- rha-10-structures — RHA §10 / 33 U.S.C. §403 (and §13 refuse) (Structures and obstructions in navigable waters): Any data-center or DC-power-plant cooling intake or outfall structure placed in a navigable river or lake needs §10 authorization on top of NPDES/§404 — a second, Sackett-proof Corps permit gate (relevant to Lake Anna-style surface-water cooling and river-supplied campuses). Example cases: US-v-Republic-Steel-RHA-1960, AWS-LakeAnnaVA-VPDES-cooling-discharge-2026.
- eqap-interstate-aquifer — EQAP U.S. Const. art. III, §2 original jurisdiction — equitable apportionment of an interstate aquifer (Equitable apportionment reaches groundwater): A data center pumping heavily from an aquifer that crosses a state line creates precisely the fact pattern this doctrine governs, and the injured party is the neighbouring *state*, not the neighbouring landowner. The practical barrier is evidentiary: an apportionment claim needs clear-and-convincing proof of real injury, which means utility-level aggregate withdrawal data — the class of data the HB 496-style reporting laws tracked in this dataset are starting to generate. Example cases: Mississippi-v-Tennessee-2021.
- eqap-commerce-clause — EQAP Dormant Commerce Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, §8, cl. 3) (Groundwater is an article of interstate commerce): Runs in the opposite direction from most doctrines here: it is the constraint on a *state* that tries to keep its water away from out-of-state data-center demand. A statute written to stop water leaving for a neighbouring state's campus is more vulnerable than one that limits large withdrawals regardless of where the user sits — which is why the durable instruments in this dataset regulate by volume and use, not by destination. Example cases: Sporhase-v-Nebraska-1982.
- ptd-reopener — PTD Public trust doctrine — continuing supervision over allocated water (No water right is immune from trust reconsideration): The doctrine that makes an already-issued water allocation reviewable. A data center supplied under a long-standing municipal or appropriative right is not insulated by that right if the resulting draw damages a trust resource — which matters because most data-center supply arrives through existing utility entitlements rather than new permits, and those are exactly what this doctrine reopens. Example cases: National-Audubon-v-Superior-Court-1983.
- ptd-groundwater-nexus — PTD Public trust doctrine as applied to groundwater extraction affecting navigable waters (The trust follows groundwater into surface flow): Closes the gap a data center's hydrology usually falls into. Campus wells are rarely regulated as a surface-water diversion, but where drawdown depletes a connected stream the trust duty attaches to the well permit itself. It also means a state groundwater-management statute is a floor, not a ceiling: complying with the statute does not answer the trust claim. Example cases: ELF-v-SWRCB-2018.
- ptd-precautionary — PTD Public trust doctrine — burden of proof and the precautionary principle (Uncertainty weighs toward protecting the resource): Directly inverts the usual posture of a data-center water fight. The recurring complaint in this dataset is that opponents cannot prove harm because consumption figures are confidential — under this reading the applicant carries the burden, and unresolved hydrology argues for the resource. Its force is jurisdiction-specific: Hawai'i's constitutional water provisions are unusually strong, so this is the ceiling of the doctrine rather than its typical reach. Example cases: Waiahole-Ditch-2000.
- gw-ownership-takings — GW Groundwater owned in place; regulation as a constitutional taking (Groundwater as a compensable property interest): Cuts both ways, which is why it belongs in the registry. It is the doctrine a data center would invoke against a withdrawal cap imposed after it acquired the land — and equally the one a neighbouring landowner invokes when a regulator permits the campus to draw down the property interest under their own acreage. It also explains why states in this family regulate through districts and permits rather than by prohibition: outright restriction carries a compensation risk. Example cases: Edwards-Aquifer-Authority-v-Day-2012.
- well-cumulative-impact — WELL State high-capacity well permitting — agency duty to consider harm to waters of the state (The permitting agency must weigh a well's off-site impact): The most practically usable doctrine in the registry for an opponent, because it operates at the permit stage rather than after the damage. It also sets the price of admission: objections to a data-center well must arrive as hydrologic evidence, since generalized concern does not trigger the agency's duty. That is precisely the bind sites in this dataset describe — the evidence needs consumption data the operator holds. Example cases: Lake-Beulah-v-DNR-2011.
- cl-negligent-subsidence — CL Negligence, willful waste and malicious injury as limits on the rule of capture (Capture shields depletion, not negligent harm): The opening in an otherwise closed door. A neighbour in a capture state cannot complain that a data center took the water, but can complain about how: well spacing, siting near a boundary, and pumping rates chosen despite engineering forecasts of subsidence. Coastal and alluvial settings are where this bites, because that is where measurable subsidence follows drawdown. Example cases: Friendswood-v-Smith-Southwest-1978.
- cl-citizen-standing-limit — CL Standing under state environmental-protection statutes — particularized injury (The standing trap for opposition groups): Explains a pattern visible across this dataset: why data-center opposition succeeds through zoning votes, moratoriums and records requests far more often than through lawsuits. A group organized around a watershed rather than around injured members can be dismissed before the merits. It also says which plaintiff wins — the household whose well failed, not the coalition, which is why the Newton County fact pattern is legally stronger than a general-harm campaign. Example cases: MCWC-v-Nestle-Waters-2007.
- util-shortage-moratorium — UTIL Municipal water service — no right to new service; moratorium review (A utility may refuse to serve a new large customer): Runs the opposite way from how these fights are usually argued. The tracked conflicts assume the utility is under pressure to say yes; this reading says a utility facing real supply constraint is on strong legal ground saying no, and the data center has no entitlement to be served. Where a utility has already conceded on the record that it cannot serve the load without major upgrades — Bessemer being the clearest instance here — that admission is the rational basis a refusal would rest on. Example cases: Swanson-v-Marin-MWD-1976.
- esa-proximate-cause-limit — ESA ESA §9 take, 16 U.S.C. §1538 — proximate cause between state permitting and downstream harm (State water permitting is usually too remote to be a take): Included as a *negative* reading, because knowing where a theory fails is worth as much as knowing where it works. ESA is the intuitive federal hook for a data center drying a river reach, and in the Fifth Circuit this is binding law that the hook will usually miss when the defendant is the state permitting authority. A §9 claim would need to run at the withdrawer directly, with a much shorter causal chain than 'permit issued, species died'. Example cases: Aransas-Project-v-Shaw-2014.
- gwmgmt-az-ama — GWMGMT Arizona Groundwater Management Act of 1980 — Active Management Areas and assured water supply (Assured-water-supply rules inside an Active Management Area): This, and not the common-law reasonable-use rule, is what an Arizona data center actually answers to, which is why Arizona fights look different from Georgia or Texas ones: the question is decided in a statutory supply-designation process rather than in a nuisance suit. It cuts both ways — the regime is a real constraint on new demand, and it also gives a project that clears it a defensible answer to critics. Example cases: ProjectBlue-Tucson-AMES-2026.
- gwmgmt-sgma — GWMGMT California Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, Cal. Water Code §10720 et seq. (Basin sustainability plans, and what they do not displace): Sets the numeric constraint a large new California groundwater user has to fit inside, and answers the compliance defence in advance. An operator pointing to its sustainability-plan allocation has not thereby answered a public-trust objection, because the two obligations coexist. Example cases: ELF-v-SWRCB-2018.
- xfer-area-of-origin — XFER Tex. Water Code §11.085 — inter-basin transfers junior in priority (Moving water between basins costs you your seniority): The sharpest and least-used tool against a campus supplied by out-of-basin piping. Opposition to these projects is usually political — hearings, petitions, county votes — when the statute already imposes a structural penalty: the transferred supply sits at the back of the priority queue exactly when drought makes it matter. Worth checking wherever a project's water arrives from a reservoir in another basin. Example cases: Rowan-ProjectCinco-Medina-TX-2025.
- tribal-winters — TRIBAL Winters doctrine — implied reservation of water, 207 U.S. 564 (1908) (Reserved rights are senior to everything that came after): Matters wherever a campus draws from a basin that also serves a reservation, which describes much of the arid Southwest. The exposure is not that a tribe sues the data center — it is that quantifying a senior reserved right shrinks the pool the state had been allocating, and junior users get cut in order. A supply contract resting on a junior state-law right is worth less than it appears in such a basin. Example cases: Winters-v-United-States-1908.
- tribal-groundwater — TRIBAL Reserved rights extend to groundwater — Agua Caliente, 849 F.3d 1262 (9th Cir. 2017) (The reserved right reaches the aquifer, not just the river): Closes the escape route. A project can be told a basin's surface water is fully claimed and turn to wells instead — this says the senior federal right follows it underground. In arid basins with a reservation overlying or adjoining the aquifer, groundwater is not the unencumbered alternative it is usually treated as. Example cases: Agua-Caliente-v-CVWD-2017.
- sepa-supply-adequacy — SEPA State environmental review — long-term water supply must be realistic, not on paper (An environmental document must show water that actually exists): The most transferable procedural attack on a data-center approval, because it does not require proving hydrologic harm — only that the paperwork assumed water it could not demonstrate. Campus approvals routinely analyse phase one and defer the rest, which is the precise defect this reading names. It is also the doctrine that most often produces the outcome opponents actually want: the approval is vacated and redone, rather than damages awarded years later. Example cases: Vineyard-v-Rancho-Cordova-2007.
- sepa-review-injunction — SEPA State environmental review — interim relief where water disclosure is inadequate (Inadequate water disclosure can stop the project now): The timing half of the supply-adequacy reading, and the reason state environmental review outranks most federal theories in practice for these projects: it can halt work while the dispute is live. Data-center construction moves faster than litigation, so a remedy that only arrives after the campus is built is not much of a remedy. Example cases: MCEA-PineIsland-MN-ProjectSkyway-2026.

## Water enforcement cases (CWA, SDWA, TSCA, RCRA, RHA)

- Meta-MorganCo-GA-investigation-2026 (2026) — SDWA — Data Center / Groundwater & aquifers / CWA potential — EPA investigation pledged — no enforcement action yet. Highest-profile potential CWA enforcement matter against a hyperscaler currently active, but at this point it is a pledged federal investigation, not an enforcement action. Distinguishing this from a closed case matters: as of late May 2026, no hyperscaler has been formally cited under CWA in this matter. The case illustrates both the regulatory attention now focused on data centers and the lag between resident complaints and formal agency action. How SDWA could apply: If construction runoff or blasting sediment reaches streams or wetlands, the §402 construction general permit applies — the Stillwater and Boydton template. If contaminants are migrating to wells via groundwater that ultimately reaches surface water, Maui's 'functional equivalent' test could require an NPDES permit; the wells themselves are Safe Drinking Water Act territory, outside the CWA. Source: https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/epa-to-investigate-meta-data-center-link-to-contaminated-water
- QTS-Fayetteville-GA-2024 (2024-2026) — CWA — Data Center / Construction stormwater / CWA applied — §402 construction GP — citizen monitoring + GA EPD. QTS Fayetteville is the clearest example of an environmental NGO using CWA construction-stormwater standards to pressure a hyperscale colocation operator. Even without a filed lawsuit, citizen documentation forced site changes — a template likely to spread, especially in Georgia where data center sprawl is concentrated in sensitive Flint and Chattahoochee basins. Source: https://myemail.constantcontact.com/Flint-Riverkeeper-Enforcement-Actions-Regarding-QTS-Data-Center-in-Fayetteville--GA.html?soid=1132272468083&aid=1tyMrrbryUM
- Nscale-MasonCounty-WV-2026 (2026) — CWA — Data Center / Construction stormwater / CWA potential — Potential §402 construction stormwater — WV DEP. The most recent and most visible 'construction stormwater fails catastrophically' incident in the data center sector. Even where the site was 'permit-compliant' the week before, AI-era buildout pace plus climate-intensified rainfall produced real-world property damage — exactly the failure mode that hardens citizen-suit pipelines and fuels stricter state CGP terms. How CWA could apply: A silt-fence/retention failure that discharges sediment off-site is the classic §402 construction-stormwater violation — WV DEP can issue an NOV under its delegated construction general permit, and downstream residents could serve a §505 citizen-suit notice. Source: https://www.wsaz.com/2026/05/24/data-center-construction-causes-severe-flooding-mason-county-residents-be-reimbursed/
- Amazon-Boardman-OR-nitrate-2026 (2024-2026) — SDWA/RCRA — Data Center / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — State-law class action — $20.5M settlement (no CWA). First and largest direct-hyperscaler water-pollution settlement in U.S. history and the only documented case where a major data center operator paid eight figures over groundwater contamination from cooling/process-water disposal. Critical precedent: hyperscalers can be held liable not just for their own discharge but for the cumulative groundwater impacts of industrial-park co-disposal arrangements — even when the actual permittee is the port authority. Dramatically expands the data-center water-liability frontier from stormwater into nitrate/nutrient land application. How SDWA/RCRA could apply: Under Maui, land-applied process water whose nitrate migrates through groundwater to the Columbia River could be the 'functional equivalent' of a direct discharge requiring a §402 NPDES permit — the same theory the Maui remand court applied to injection wells. Source: https://www.opb.org/article/2026/03/31/amazon-fine-northeast-oregon-boardman-nitrate-pollution-well/
- ProjectBlue-Tucson-AMES-2026 (2026) — SDWA/GWMGMT — Data Center / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — Municipal water denial + CAA dust NOV (no CWA). Highlights the convergence of CWA-adjacent stormwater/dust control, municipal water-permit politics, and groundwater extraction permitting at a single hyperscale site. Tucson is the first major U.S. city to formally deny municipal water service to a data center on policy grounds — a precedent that may shift hyperscale projects toward private groundwater wells subject to state withdrawal permits rather than CWA-regulated discharges. How SDWA/GWMGMT could apply: The CWA has no handle on a municipal water-service denial. The construction site itself still carries §402 stormwater obligations — sediment or dust-suppression runoff leaving the site would be enforceable the way Stillwater and Boydton were. Source: https://www.kgun9.com/news/local-news/contractor-working-on-project-blue-data-center-issued-notice-of-violation
- Google-ProjectRaspberry-VA-2026 (2025-2026) — CWA — Data Center / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — §404 individual permit application (in federal review). One of the largest §404 individual permit applications for a single data center campus currently in the federal pipeline in Virginia. The FOIA fight over water-use projections (8 MGD/day at full buildout) is itself precedent-setting: Virginia courts confirmed that data center water-use records held by public utilities are public records, not proprietary business information — a significant transparency ruling for the tracker's data-collection strategy. Source: https://www.nao.usace.army.mil/Media/Public-Notices/Article/4428952/nao-2025-01857-project-raspberry-botetourt-virginia/
- Google-ProjectLoch-VA-2026 (2026) — CWA — Data Center / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — §404 individual permit application (in federal review). Together with Project Raspberry (NAO-2025-01857) and the Little Rock AR application, Google's concurrent §404 permit applications in Virginia show that hyperscaler data center construction is generating a wave of individual §404 permits in the federal pipeline — each with multi-acre wetland and multi-thousand-foot stream impacts. The cumulative wetland/stream impact of Virginia's data center build-out is now large enough to warrant cumulative-impact analysis under NEPA. Source: https://www.nao.usace.army.mil/Media/Public-Notices/Article/4484789/nao-2026-00182-vmrc-project-loch-chesterfield-county-virginia-wauford-prm-site/
- Google-LittleRock-AR-2026 (2026) — CWA — Data Center / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — §404 individual permit application (in federal review). The largest single §404 wetland impact in any active data center permit application, illustrating that hyperscale campuses can generate wetland and stream impacts an order of magnitude larger than construction stormwater GPs alone address. The 16.8-acre/6,000-foot footprint is a credible trigger for individual permit review rather than nationwide permits, giving the Corps and state §401 certifying authority substantial leverage over project design. Source: https://www.swl.usace.army.mil/Missions/Regulatory/Public-Notices/Article/4447433/swl-2026-00038/

Hyperscalers are beginning to seek their own direct NPDES/VPDES discharge permits rather than routing all cooling water through municipal WWTPs — moving the operational CWA exposure from the receiving POTW's permit onto the data center itself. Transparency litigation by Waterkeeper-affiliated groups is becoming the soft-enforcement lever where no discharge violation yet exists. How CWA could apply: Where the filled wetlands are federally jurisdictional (post-Sackett: continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters, plausible this close to Lake Michigan tributaries), the fill requires federal §404 authorization and a §401 certification, coordinated through Wisconsin's individual-permit process — the same posture as Amazon's New Carlisle campus one state south.
