Captures how Iowa DNR + Iowa AG handle large industrial users that overload small-town POTWs — including the indirect harm of forcing a municipal WWTP offline. Directly relevant to the West Des Moines / Altoona Microsoft data center cluster: pretreatment-violation enforcement against a single large industrial customer of a city WWTP sets the template for how Iowa would respond if a data center's chemical-treatment effluent disrupted a host municipality's treatment plant. Source: https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2025/07/30/iowa-attorney-general-settles-dnr-cases-for-agri-star-and-nishnabotna-river-pollution/
- Youngstown-OH-CSO-2025 (2002-2025) — CWA — Industrial Water / Treatment plants & sewers (POTW) / CWA applied — §301/§402 CSO consent decree (modified). Older Midwestern combined-sewer cities cannot meet original CSO long-term control schedules without modification — and Section 301 liability continues to attach during the renegotiation. For data centers locating in older industrial cities (e.g., Youngstown, Hartford, Columbus' equivalents), the POTW operator is already under federal supervision, which means new industrial users face accelerated pretreatment scrutiny and likely capital surcharges. Source: https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/consent-decree-city-youngstown-ohio-sewer-overflows-settlement
- MDC-Hartford-CT-CSO-2025 (2006-2025) — CWA — Industrial Water / Treatment plants & sewers (POTW) / CWA applied — §301/§402 SSO consent decree (modified). Reinforces a now-well-established federal-court pattern in older Northeastern cities: CSO consent decrees stretch >25 years and require multi-billion-dollar capital outlays. Any large new industrial user (including data centers) discharging to such a system adds cost pressure on an already-strained system, making POTW pretreatment programs tighter. Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/23/2025-01559/notice-of-lodging-of-proposed-first-amended-consent-decree-under-the-clean-water-act
- Wynja-Feedlot-IA-CAFO-2025 (2021-2025) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §301(a) unpermitted CAFO discharge — penalty. Demonstrates that operating any industrial facility without an NPDES permit when discharges occur is independently actionable under Section 301(a), regardless of pollutant concentrations — a small-penalty but precedent-establishing CAFO case. The parallel for data centers: cooling tower blowdown to surface water or land application without an active NPDES permit (or coverage under a general permit like Ohio's draft OHD000001) is the same per-day violation. Source: https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/wynja-feedlot-settlement-information-sheet
- Oklahoma-v-Tyson-IRW-2005-2025 (2005-2025) — CWA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / No CWA action — State public-nuisance judgment (no CWA). Lands a landmark long-tail public-nuisance precedent on land-applied industrial waste that escapes NPDES coverage via the agricultural-stormwater exemption — directly relevant to data centers whose cooling-tower blowdown is land-applied through municipal reuse programs (e.g., Loudoun Water reclaimed water deliveries). State common-law nuisance can fill the federal CWA gap when EPA enforcement is unavailable. How CWA could apply: The agricultural-stormwater exemption keeps land-applied litter runoff out of §402. Land application of *industrial* or municipal-reuse water enjoys no such exemption — under Maui, nutrient migration to streams could require an NPDES permit, which is why this nuisance route matters for reclaimed-water cooling programs. Source: https://www.oklahomafarmreport.com/okfr/2025/12/20/federal-judge-orders-poultry-integrators-to-fund-30-year-remediation-of-illinois-river-watershed/
- Tyco-BASF-PFAS-AFFF-PWS-2024 (2024-2025) — SDWA/TSCA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / No CWA action — Mass-tort drinking-water settlements (no CWA). PFAS dischargers face product-liability exposure that dwarfs typical CWA civil penalties — particularly relevant if data center cooling-water additives or fire-suppression systems (many use AFFF or AFFF-substitute foams) become tied to PFAS contamination findings. Data centers using PFAS-containing fluorochemical fire suppression face latent decades-long mass-tort exposure on the Tyco/BASF model. How SDWA/TSCA could apply: AFFF releases reaching surface water are actionable as §311 hazardous-substance spills, and Chemours shows PFAS in effluent is already enforceable under §402 NPDES limits; EPA's pending PFAS effluent guidelines would make this routine. Source: https://www.basf.com/us/en/media/news-releases/2024/05/basf-corporation-enters-class-settlement-with-u-s--public-water-
- Greenidge-SenecaLake-NY-2025 (2021-2025) — CWA — Industrial Water / Cooling water & thermal (§316) / CWA applied — §316(a)/(b) + SPDES — thermal/intake findings. The only documented case where a digital-infrastructure operator (bitcoin mining / high-density compute) faces formal §316(a) thermal-discharge exceedance findings and unresolved §316(b) intake noncompliance. The 139 MGD intake volume is comparable to a large industrial cooling system. Data centers using once-through or open-loop cooling on surface-water intakes face the same §316(b) best-technology-available and §316(a) thermal-variance obligations — Greenidge illustrates what enforcement looks like when those obligations are not met. Source: https://waterfrontonline.blog/2022/10/07/greenidges-warm-water-discharges-heated-seneca-lake-beyond-state-limits-but-dec-wavier-excuses-violations/
- Norfolk-Southern-East-Palestine-2024 (2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / CWA applied — §311 spill — $15M CWA penalty. Establishes the statutory ceiling of $15M as the EPA/DOJ benchmark for a single catastrophic CWA spill event, while showing that the real bite comes from response-cost recovery and long-tail monitoring obligations. For data centers, the parallel risk is a single transformer-oil or PFAS-firefighting-foam release that triggers CERCLA + CWA liability layered together. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/united-states-reaches-over-310-million-settlement-norfolk-southern-address-harms
- Cahokia-Heights-2024 (2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Treatment plants & sewers (POTW) / CWA applied — §301 unpermitted SSOs — consent decree. Reinforces that even small/distressed POTWs can be forced into $30M+ federal compliance regimes — meaning any data center siting in an environmental-justice sewer service area should expect heavily scrutinized pretreatment terms. Also shows EPA's willingness to litigate against under-resourced systems, which raises pretreatment-permit issuance risk for new industrial users. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-and-doj-announce-settlement-cahokia-heights-illinois-improper-operation-citys-0
- Guam-Waterworks-2024 (2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Treatment plants & sewers (POTW) / CWA applied — §402 SSO/NPDES consent decree. Especially relevant because the decree explicitly requires the POTW to tighten its industrial pretreatment program — the exact lever that municipal sewer authorities will pull when faced with high-volume new users like data centers. Demonstrates a pattern where federal sewer-system decrees translate directly into tougher pretreatment terms for industrial customers. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/united-states-reaches-agreement-guam-waterworks-authority-requiring-investment-sewer
- Denali-Water-Solutions-2024 (2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Treatment plants & sewers (POTW) / CWA applied — §405 sludge + §301 — judicial action. First-of-its-kind judicial precedent that EPA will litigate over biosolids/sludge management — which matters because many large data-center POTWs ultimately dispose of treatment-plant biosolids contaminated with PFAS and other industrial inputs. Data center pretreatment violations that send PFAS or metals into POTW sludge can trigger downstream Section 405 exposure for the receiving POTW. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/denali-water-solutions-llc-pay-610k-alleged-illegal-sewage-sludge-application
- Reading-WWTP-2024 (2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Sewer pretreatment (§307) / CWA applied — §402 + §307 pretreatment-program consent decree. Squarely on-point: the decree centers on a POTW's failure to enforce its pretreatment program against industrial users — the exact regulatory mechanism that controls data-center cooling-water and process-water discharge. POTWs operating under such decrees are required to tighten industrial-user oversight, which translates into stricter pretreatment permits, monitoring, and enforcement against high-volume industrial customers like data centers. Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/01/31/2024-01883/notice-of-lodging-of-consent-decree-under-the-clean-water-act
- Republic-Steel-OH-2024 (2017-2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §402 NPDES — joint federal-state action. Demonstrates that long-running industrial NPDES exceedances on small Ohio receiving streams (Nimishillen Creek) draw multi-year federal-state enforcement scrutiny. Relevant to Licking County / central Ohio data center buildout where cooling-water and stormwater discharges feed into similarly modest creeks; per-day penalty exposure ($67K/day sought) sets a Region 5 precedent that would apply to any data center NPDES non-compliance. Source: https://www.wkyc.com/article/money/business/republic-steel-700k-fine-epa-lawsuit-water-pollution-canton-lorain-plants/95-3a62f87f-c45b-4286-ae47-212fd57fbaaa
- Energix-VA-2024 (2022-2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Construction stormwater / CWA applied — §402 VAR10 construction GP — escalating DEQ fines. Sets a direct VADEQ enforcement precedent for large-footprint Virginia construction projects with VAR10 stormwater general permits — exactly the regulatory regime under which Loudoun and Prince William data center campuses are built. Three consecutive years of escalating fines signal VADEQ will use repeat-violator escalation on developers who treat E&S controls as a paperwork exercise. Source: https://cardinalnews.org/2024/05/21/solar-firm-energix-fined-again-for-virginia-environmental-violations/
- Pactiv-Evergreen-Canton-NC-2023-2024 (2021-2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §402 NPDES — NC DEQ civil penalties. Illustrates how NC DEQ uses repeated Civil Penalty Assessments and toxicity-based exceedances to enforce against a major industrial NPDES discharger on a small mountain receiving stream. Relevant to North Carolina data center proposals (e.g., Lenoir, Maiden corridor) where cooling discharges to similar small receiving waters would face the same per-day NOV/CPA framework. Source: https://www.bpr.org/bpr-news/2023-08-11/canton-paper-mill-receives-second-chemical-violation-this-summer
- SpaceX-Starbase-TX-2024 (2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §402/TPDES unpermitted discharge — TCEQ + EPA. Underscores that industrial cooling/process-water discharges — even from non-traditional sources like rocket deluge systems — fall squarely under TPDES jurisdiction in Texas. Highly relevant to San Antonio and Austin-area hyperscale data centers using evaporative cooling: any unpermitted blowdown or stormwater conveyance carrying industrial water can trigger TCEQ Agreed Orders without prior NOV. Source: https://www.cnbc.com/2024/08/12/spacex-repeatedly-polluted-waters-in-texas-tceq-epa-found.html
- Hyponex-Scotts-OH-2024 (2020-2024) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §402 NPDES — EPA Region 5 + Ohio EPA. Direct Region 5 + Ohio EPA precedent for industrial NPDES exceedances on small Ohio tributaries — the receiving-water profile that matches Licking County / New Albany data center stormwater outfalls and any future Ohio data center cooling-water discharges under the in-development OHD000001 general permit. Shows that even relatively modest, time-bounded exceedances at a non-data-center industrial facility draw six-figure CAFO penalties. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-reaches-100000-settlement-hyponex-corp-alleged-clean-water-act-violations-shreve
- Westchester-JointWaterWorks-NY-SDWA-filtration-2024 (2019-2024) — SDWA — Industrial Water / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — SDWA Part B consent decree — public water system filtration/treatment, $600K penalty. Demonstrates how long-deferred SDWA filtration/treatment obligations at a public water system escalate into nine-figure capital consent-decree liability — directly relevant where data-center-driven demand growth strains a regional water utility's aging treatment infrastructure and delays compliance investment, the same supply-capacity fact pattern already tracked at Bessemer, AL and Richland Parish, LA. How SDWA could apply: A regional water utility whose treatment infrastructure lags fast-growing (including data-center-driven) demand risks the same SDWA filtration/treatment-technique violations, escalating from administrative order to a multi-hundred-million-dollar federal consent decree. Source: https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/westchester-joint-water-works-safe-drinking-water-act-consent-decree-westchester-county
- CJTGroup-Georgia-PWS-disinfectant-emergency-2024 (2024) — SDWA — Industrial Water / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — SDWA §1431 emergency administrative order. A small, thinly-capitalized private water-system operator is exactly the ownership profile increasingly asked to absorb new industrial and data-center-adjacent hookup demand in fast-growing exurban Georgia — this order shows how quickly a routine disinfection-residual lapse becomes a federal emergency action. How SDWA could apply: Georgia's exurban data-center corridor (Fayette, Newton, Coweta, Morgan counties, all already in this dataset) is served by a patchwork of small private/municipal water systems; the same §1431 emergency-order mechanism used here reaches any system whose capacity or maintenance is compromised by rapid nearby industrial growth. Source: https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/national-enforcement-and-compliance-initiative-increasing-compliance-drinking-water-0
- Chemours-Washington-Works-PFAS-2023 (2023) — CWA/TSCA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / CWA applied — §402 NPDES PFAS effluent limits — consent agreement. First federal precedent that PFAS discharges in effluent and stormwater are directly actionable under Clean Water Act NPDES authority — not just CERCLA. Data centers use PFAS-containing immersion cooling fluids and aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) firefighting agents; once EPA's promised PFAS NPDES application rule is in place, any data-center stormwater outfall that tests positive becomes a potential enforcement target on this template. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-takes-first-ever-federal-clean-water-act-enforcement-action-address-pfas
- Hailiang-Copper-TX-2023 (2023) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §402/TPDES unauthorized discharge — TCEQ penalty. Direct precedent for TCEQ penalty methodology when an industrial facility releases process water beyond permit authorization. Penalties scale with discharge volume; relevant to Texas data center sites where heat-exchanger blowdown or chemical-treatment volumes could similarly exceed permitted volumes. Shows TCEQ's expedited settlement mechanism gives modest dollar penalties for one-off bulk discharges relative to ongoing exceedances. Source: https://www.tceq.texas.gov/downloads/agency/decisions/agendas/backup/2023/2023-0715-iwd-e.pdf
- Cleveland-Cliffs-Burns-Harbor-2022 (2022) — CWA — Industrial Water / Cooling water & thermal (§316) / CWA applied — §402 NPDES — penalty after cooling-loop failure. Establishes a benchmark for million-dollar federal penalties when a cooling-loop/process-water system fails and an industrial facility is forced to discharge uncontrolled volumes through its NPDES outfalls. Data centers with closed-loop chilled-water systems face an analogous failure mode if cooling-tower blowdown or condensate exceeds POTW pretreatment or NPDES limits during an upset. Source: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/cleveland-cliffs-agrees-improve-environmental-compliance-indiana-facility-and-pay-3
- American-Zinc-Recycling-Palmerton-2021 (2014-2021) — CWA — Industrial Water / Cooling water & thermal (§316) / CWA applied — §402 NPDES contact cooling water — settlement. Most direct cooling-water analog in EPA's enforcement docket: a contact-cooling-water stream that picked up metals (zinc, cadmium) from process equipment and violated NPDES limits. Data centers using closed-loop systems with copper piping or biocide additives can produce blowdown with similar metal/pH profiles — and would face the same NPDES exceedance liability if discharged directly or under a pretreatment permit. Source: https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/american-zinc-recycling-corp-settlement
- Plains-Pipeline-Santa-Barbara-2020 (2020) — CWA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / CWA applied — §311 oil spill — ~$24M federal penalty. Sets a benchmark of ~$24M federal penalty for an industrial oil discharge to navigable waters and shows how natural-resource damages stack on top of CWA Section 311 civil penalties. For data centers, this matters because backup-generator and transformer-oil reservoirs are CWA-regulated 'oil' under SPCC and could trigger Section 311 liability on top of NPDES penalties if discharged to a waterway. Source: https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/houston-based-plains-pipeline-spend-more-44-million-resolve-clean-water-act-violations
- Yuengling-Pottsville-2016 (2008-2016) — CWA — Industrial Water / Sewer pretreatment (§307) / CWA applied — §307 pretreatment — consent decree. Closest legal analog to a data-center cooling-water situation: an industrial user discharging to a municipal POTW under a local pretreatment permit. Persistent permit exceedances — even without direct surface-water discharge — generate eight-figure compliance costs. Data centers in Loudoun, Prince William, and Central Ohio that send cooling-tower blowdown to wholesale POTWs sit in the same regulatory posture. Source: https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/dg-yuengling-and-son-inc-clean-water-act-settlement
- Swift-Beef-Grand-Island-2011 (2006-2011) — CWA — Industrial Water / Sewer pretreatment (§307) / CWA applied — §307 pretreatment — consent decree. Directly relevant model for data centers discharging cooling-tower blowdown to municipal sewers: pretreatment-program violations (interference / pass-through at the POTW) are independently enforceable under CWA 307, even when the data center itself holds no direct NPDES permit. Repeat offenders see escalating penalties. Source: https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/swift-beef-company-pay-13-million-penalty-clean-water-act-and-state-law-violations-its-grand
- DuPont-WashingtonWorks-PFOA-2005-2009 (2002-2009) — SDWA/TSCA/RCRA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / No CWA action — TSCA §8(e) $10.25M penalty + SDWA §1431 consent orders (no CWA). The definitive multi-statute water case: when the CWA's permit machinery had nothing to say about an unregulated contaminant, EPA reached the same fact pattern through TSCA (concealed risk data) and SDWA Section 1431 (drinking-water endangerment). For data centers, this is the playbook if a cooling-chemistry constituent or fuel-farm release turns up in neighbors' wells — no NPDES violation is needed for EPA to order alternative water and treatment. How SDWA/TSCA/RCRA could apply: The CWA reaches this fact pattern only once PFAS effluent limits enter NPDES permits — which is exactly what later happened at the same plant (see the 2023 Chemours Washington Works consent agreement). Until a pollutant is permit-regulated, TSCA reporting and SDWA §1431 are the operative federal hooks. Source: https://www.epa.gov/archive/epapages/newsroom_archive/newsreleases/fdcb2f665cac66bb852570d7005d6665.html
- Brayton-Point-Dominion-2003-2007 (2003-2007) — CWA — Industrial Water / Cooling water & thermal (§316) / CWA applied — §316(a)/(b) — NPDES forced closed-cycle retrofit. Most important precedent for evaporative-cooled data centers: 316(b) BTA can require retrofitting once-through cooling to closed-cycle (i.e., cooling towers), making intake design a regulated variable for any facility withdrawing more than ~2 MGD. Future large data centers drawing from surface water will face the same BTA analysis. Source: https://www.epa.gov/npdes-permits/brayton-point-station-power-plant-somerset-ma-final-npdes-permit
- 3M-TSCA-8e-PFAS-2006 (2006) — TSCA — Industrial Water / Spills, PFAS & contamination / No CWA action — TSCA reporting settlement — $1.52M, 244 counts (no CWA). Extends the DuPont lesson up the supply chain: chemical manufacturers whose products end up in industrial water systems (biocides, corrosion inhibitors, fluorochemical surfactants, AFFF) carry their own federal reporting duty. Water advocates near data-center campuses can leverage TSCA disclosures to trace contaminants found in wells or effluent back to a supplier. How TSCA could apply: Same trajectory as DuPont: the CWA attaches later, when PFAS monitoring and limits appear in NPDES permits and in POTW pretreatment local limits — at which point historical TSCA disclosures become the evidence base. Source: https://www.epa.gov/archive/epapages/newsroom_archive/newsreleases/440f8e8e3e28707e8525715b007186f7.html
- Tyson-Sedalia-2003 (1996-2003) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §309(c) criminal — felony plea. Demonstrates that knowing discharge in violation of an NPDES permit (or knowingly falsified DMRs) can be charged as a felony under CWA 309(c), not just a civil matter. Cooling-water dischargers — including data centers — that under-report blowdown concentrations risk criminal exposure for individuals as well as the corporation. Source: https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/2003/June/03_enrd_383.htm
- EPA-UIC-ClassV-MotorVehicleWells-1999 (1999-2000) — CWA/SDWA — Industrial Water / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — SDWA UIC Class V rule — well subclasses banned/permitted (no CWA). Directly regulates common data-center campus infrastructure that never touches the CWA: stormwater drywells and infiltration galleries (subclass 5D), cooling-water return-flow wells (5A) for geothermal or aquifer thermal cooling, and subsurface disposal of treated effluent are all Class V injection wells. An inland campus over a shallow aquifer answers to the UIC program even with zero surface-water discharge. How CWA/SDWA could apply: Where an injection well's fluid reaches surface water through groundwater, County of Maui adds a CWA §402 permit requirement on top of UIC authorization — the two programs overlap on subsurface disposal at campuses near streams. Source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1999-12-07/html/99-31048.htm
- Smithfield-Pagan-River-1997 (1991-1997) — CWA — Industrial Water / Industrial discharge (§402) / CWA applied — §402 NPDES — $12.6M civil judgment. Establishes that chronic NPDES-limit exceedances and inaccurate Discharge Monitoring Reports trigger per-day, per-parameter civil penalties that can reach into the eight figures. Data centers self-reporting cooling-tower-blowdown DMRs face the same per-violation penalty exposure under 33 U.S.C. 1319(d). Source: https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/1997/August97/331enr.htm
- SF-EPA-end-result-2025 (2025) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / CWA applied — SCOTUS ruling — bars 'end-result' NPDES permit terms. Data centers whose cooling-tower blowdown or stormwater discharges run through municipal POTWs or hold direct NPDES permits can no longer be hit with open-ended 'don't violate water-quality standards' language; EPA and delegated state agencies must instead set numeric or technology-based effluent limits, increasing permit predictability but shifting the regulatory burden back to permit writers. Source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/604/23-753/
- PortOfTacoma-v-PugetSoundkeeper-9thCir-2024 (2024-2025) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / CWA applied — §505 citizen-suit scope (9th Cir.). Confirms environmental groups can sue in federal court to enforce state NPDES permit terms stricter than federal law — directly raising citizen-suit exposure for the receiving WWTPs whose state-issued permits this pipeline already tracks, and for any facility operating under a state discharge permit. Source: https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/supreme-court-declines-to-hear-cases-seeking-to-narrow-citizen-suit-enforcement-in-federal-environmental-case-leaving-doors-wide-open
- CERF-v-Naples-9thCir-2024 (2024-2025) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / CWA applied — §505 mootness (9th Cir.). Narrows when CWA citizen suits can proceed: once a discharger obtains a permit or otherwise cures a violation, the Ninth Circuit treats penalty-only claims as moot — a permit-shield-style defense a data center or its receiving WWTP could invoke after coming into compliance, blunting citizen-suit deterrence. Source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2025/11/05/23-55469.pdf
- Flint-MI-SDWA-1431-2016 (2016-2025) — SDWA — Landmark Precedent / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — SDWA §1431 emergency order — nine-year federal oversight (no CWA). The most prominent modern use of SDWA emergency powers, and the proof that EPA can act directly when a drinking-water system fails its users — including where the failure is driven by cost pressure on a stressed municipal system. Relevant to any community whose small water system takes on hyperscale demand: Section 1431 is the federal backstop if supply or treatment integrity slips. How SDWA could apply: None needed — SDWA is the operative statute for drinking-water endangerment. Included here because the tracker's water-supply fights (Bessemer, Richland Parish, Charlotte) all pose the question Flint answered: what happens federally when a municipal system is pushed past its capacity to deliver safe water. Source: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-01/documents/1_21_sdwa_1431_emergency_admin_order_012116.pdf
- Loper-Bright-Enterprises-v-Raimondo-2024 (2024) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / No CWA action — APA ruling — not itself a CWA case. Direct relevance to data-center water tracking: every EPA interpretation of Section 402 (NPDES), Section 401 (state certification), Section 404 (dredge-and-fill), and the post-Sackett WOTUS rule is now reviewable de novo. EPA cannot rely on agency-deference to defend novel cooling-water effluent guidelines or technology-based limits for data centers — any future rulemaking targeting hyperscale cooling water (Ohio's draft OHD000001, Virginia's data-center reporting bills, EPA's MSGP 2026) faces a heightened judicial-review standard. How CWA could apply: Not a water case — but every CWA permit writer now loses Chevron deference, so each NPDES, §404, or WOTUS interpretation in the cases here is reviewable de novo. It applies to the CWA through every other case in this record. Source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/22-451_7m58.pdf
- Sackett-v-EPA-2023 (2023) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — SCOTUS ruling — §404/WOTUS jurisdiction narrowed. Sackett dramatically shrank federal CWA jurisdiction over wetlands, ephemeral streams, and isolated waters — the exact categories most likely to receive stormwater runoff or graywater seepage from a large data center campus. After Sackett, many data center sites that previously needed §402 NPDES or §404 permits for site drainage now fall to state-only regulation, shifting the compliance burden to state programs in Virginia and Ohio. Source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/21-454_4g15.pdf
- SierraClub-WVDEP-401-2023 (2023) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — §401 state certification vacated (4th Cir.). For data-center developers whose campuses involve federally permitted stream or wetland crossings (e.g., long-haul fiber, water-supply pipelines, electrical transmission corridors), state § 401 certifications must rest on documented project-specific anti-degradation review and explicit stormwater conditions — a boilerplate 'reasonable assurance' memo is now legally vulnerable in the Fourth Circuit, which covers Virginia. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca4/22-1008/22-1008-2023-04-03.html
- Lewis-v-United-States-5th-Cir-2023 (2023) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — §404 jurisdiction — Sackett applied (5th Cir.). First federal appellate application of Sackett to a real-world Section 404 wetlands jurisdictional dispute. The Fifth Circuit's refusal to remand sets a precedent that lower courts can apply Sackett's continuous-surface-connection test directly without Corps deference — accelerating the practical contraction of CWA jurisdiction. For data center sites that were previously subject to Section 404 wetlands mitigation (a routine cost item for Northern Virginia and Loudoun County sites), Lewis confirms the post-Sackett framework where many isolated and headwater wetlands now fall outside CWA jurisdiction and outside developer mitigation obligations. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca5/21-30163/21-30163-2023-12-18.html
- Maui-remand-DHaw-2021 (2021) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / CWA applied — §402 functional-equivalent test applied on remand. Data centers that inject cooling-tower blowdown into the subsurface, rely on percolation ponds, or send PFAS-laden effluent to land-application systems near surface water cannot assume groundwater conveyance immunizes them from NPDES requirements; short distances and traceable pollutants will trigger Maui's functional-equivalent test. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/hawaii/hidce/1:2012cv00198/102885/468/
- Mississippi-v-Tennessee-2021 (2021) — EQAP — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — SCOTUS original jurisdiction — equitable apportionment extended to groundwater. The single most directly applicable precedent to a US data-center water fight. The aquifer it governs is the same Memphis Sand that xAI's Colossus campus draws on, so the legal question of who may complain about heavy pumping there is already answered: the remedy is an interstate apportionment suit, brought by a state, not a damages claim for stolen water. The practical obstacle is evidentiary — an apportioning court needs clear and convincing proof of real injury, which requires exactly the aggregate withdrawal data that data-center water reporting laws produce. How EQAP could apply: No federal water statute was involved. The pathway to a data-center fact pattern runs through a *state* suing another state over a shared aquifer that a large industrial user is drawing down — which requires a state willing to sue and aggregate withdrawal data adequate to prove injury. Source: https://www.scotusblog.com/cases/case-files/mississippi-v-tennessee
- County-of-Maui-v-Hawaii-Wildlife-Fund-2020 (2020) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / CWA applied — SCOTUS ruling — §402 'functional equivalent' test. Directly relevant to data centers that send cooling tower blowdown, evaporative bleed, or treated process water to on-site leach fields, injection wells, or lined-but-permeable ponds rather than to a municipal sewer. If that water reaches a navigable water in a short distance/time, Maui says a federal §402 permit is required even with no pipe to the surface — a live issue for desert/inland Virginia and Ohio sites. Source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-260_jifl.pdf
- ELF-v-SWRCB-2018 (2018) — PTD/GWMGMT — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — Cal. Court of Appeal — public trust reaches groundwater pumping. The reading that reaches the ordinary data-center hydrology. Campus wells are usually regulated, if at all, as groundwater — not as a diversion from the stream they actually deplete. ELF closes that gap wherever drawdown is connected to surface flow, and it puts the duty on the *county* issuing the well permit, which is the level of government most data-center siting fights are already being fought at. It also establishes that satisfying a state groundwater statute is a floor, not a defence. How PTD/GWMGMT could apply: A challenge to the county well permit behind a data-center campus, on the ground that drawdown depletes a connected navigable stream. Requires hydrologic evidence of the groundwater-to-surface-water connection. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2018/c083239.html
- Agua-Caliente-v-CVWD-2017 (2017) — TRIBAL — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — 9th Cir. — reserved rights extend to groundwater; state law preempted. Removes the assumption that groundwater is the unencumbered fallback. A project told a basin's surface water is spoken for will look to wells; in the Ninth Circuit, a senior federal reserved right follows it there. That matters directly for the Southwest data-center corridor, where the surface supply is over-allocated, groundwater is the growth path, and reservations overlie or adjoin many of the aquifers involved. The exposure runs through the supply contract rather than through any conduct by the operator. How TRIBAL could apply: Applies where a campus's groundwater supply sits in a basin with an overlying or adjoining reservation. The claim runs between the tribe and the water district, but the resulting quantification determines what is left for the district's industrial customers. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/15-55896/15-55896-2017-03-07.html
- Aransas-Project-v-Shaw-2014 (2014) — ESA — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / No CWA action — 5th Cir. — state water permitting too remote to proximately cause an ESA take. Carried here as a *negative* precedent, because a registry that only collects theories that work will mislead. The Endangered Species Act is the intuitive federal hook when a data center's draw dries a river reach, and in the Fifth Circuit this is binding law that the hook will usually miss when the defendant is the permitting agency. A viable §9 claim has to target the withdrawer directly with a far shorter causal chain. It bears directly on the Texas Gulf-coast sites tracked here, which sit in the same hydrology and the same circuit. How ESA could apply: Marks where an ESA theory fails rather than where it works: suing the permitting agency for downstream species harm is foreclosed in this circuit. A claim would have to run against the withdrawing facility itself. Source: https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions%5Cpub%5C13/13-40317-CV0.pdf
- Edwards-Aquifer-Authority-v-Day-2012 (2012) — GW — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — Tex. Supreme Court — groundwater owned in place; regulation may be a taking. The doctrine that constrains how far a state can regulate data-center pumping in ownership-in-place jurisdictions, and it points both ways. An operator that bought land can assert a property interest against a withdrawal cap imposed afterwards; a neighbour whose water is drawn out from under them holds the same kind of interest against a regulator that permitted the campus. It also explains an otherwise puzzling pattern in this dataset — why Texas fights run through conservation-district permits and local politics rather than through outright prohibition, since prohibition carries a compensation bill. How GW could apply: Two routes to a data-center fact pattern: as the operator's defence against a new withdrawal cap, and as an injured neighbour's theory against the district that permitted the drawdown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Aquifer_Authority_v._Day_and_McDaniel
- Lake-Beulah-v-DNR-2011 (2011) — WELL — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — Wis. Supreme Court — agency duty to consider well impacts on waters of the state. The most directly usable doctrine here for anyone contesting a data-center well, because it operates before the water is pumped rather than after the harm. It also states the price of admission plainly: objections must arrive as hydrologic evidence, not as concern. That is the bind these conflicts keep hitting — the evidence needed to trigger the duty depends on consumption and drawdown data the operator and the utility hold. Wisconsin makes this concrete for the tracker, since Microsoft's Mount Pleasant campus sits in the same permitting system. How WELL could apply: Reaches a data center at the well-permit stage: a challenge to the state agency for issuing without evaluating impact, which succeeds only if objectors put concrete hydrologic evidence in front of the agency first. Source: https://www.wicourts.gov/sc/opinion/DisplayDocument.pdf?content=pdf&seqNo=67354
- Entergy-v-Riverkeeper-2009 (2009) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Cooling water & thermal (§316) / CWA applied — SCOTUS ruling — §316(b) cost-benefit allowed. Most data centers don't trigger §316(b) directly — it applies to intakes designed to withdraw more than 2 MGD from waters of the US for cooling, and the vast majority of data centers buy potable water from municipal utilities. But Entergy's broader cost-benefit doctrine carries over to EPA standard-setting under other CWA provisions, including any future effluent guidelines or §304(m) rules aimed at data center cooling discharges or PFAS-bearing immersion-cooling fluids. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/07-588.ZS.html
- MCWC-v-Nestle-Waters-2007 (2007) — CL — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / No CWA action — Mich. Supreme Court — MEPA standing requires particularized injury. The procedural reason so much data-center opposition in this dataset runs through zoning votes, moratoriums and records requests rather than litigation: a watershed coalition can lose before the merits are reached. It also identifies the right plaintiff. A household whose own well failed has the particularized injury a coalition lacks, which is why the Newton County fact pattern is a stronger case than a general-harm campaign against a larger withdrawal. Michigan matters directly here — its 2026 data-center bills would create the withdrawal permits such a suit would contest. How CL could apply: Governs who may bring a state environmental claim against a data-center withdrawal at all. The pathway is defensive: it is the doctrine an operator invokes to dismiss an opposition group before the merits. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/michigan/supreme-court/2007/20070725-s130802-168-nestle130802-op.html
- Vineyard-v-Rancho-Cordova-2007 (2007) — SEPA — Landmark Precedent / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — Cal. Supreme Court — EIR must show a realistic long-term water supply. The most transferable procedural attack on a data-center approval anywhere with a state environmental review statute, because it needs no proof of hydrologic harm — only that the document assumed water it could not demonstrate. Campus approvals routinely analyse the first phase and defer the rest to a future regional plan, which is exactly the defect named here. It also produces the remedy opponents usually want: the approval is vacated and redone before construction, rather than damages long afterward. How SEPA could apply: A challenge to the environmental document behind a data-center approval on the ground that it analysed only near-term supply and deferred the rest. Requires a state environmental review statute with a supply-analysis requirement, not a federal hook. Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/summary/opinion/ca-supreme-court/2007/02/01/147286.html
- Rapanos-v-United-States-2006 (2006) — CWA — Landmark Precedent / Wetlands & streams (§404/§401) / CWA applied — SCOTUS ruling — WOTUS plurality (pre-Sackett). Rapanos is the doctrinal precursor to Sackett: lower courts and EPA generally applied Kennedy's broader 'significant nexus' test, which kept a wide universe of wetlands and intermittent streams within federal jurisdiction. For data centers, Rapanos meant that ditches, retention ponds, and intermittent streams crossing campus sites were often federally regulated — a regime now superseded by Sackett's narrower surface-connection rule. Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-supreme-court/547/715.html
- US-v-Alisal-Water-Corp-2005 (1997-2005) — SDWA — Landmark Precedent / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — SDWA civil action — receivership + divestiture affirmed (no CWA). Establishes the outer edge of SDWA enforcement: chronic drinking-water violators can lose the utility itself, not just pay penalties. If a private or investor-owned system serving a data-center corridor cuts corners while absorbing hyperscale demand, receivership and forced divestiture are on the table. How SDWA could apply: None — SDWA is the operative statute for public-water-system integrity; this is the enforcement ceiling for the utilities that serve data-center corridors. Source: https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/2004/May/04_enrd_367.htm
- Interfaith-v-Honeywell-RCRA-2003-2005 (2003-2005) — RCRA — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — RCRA §7002 citizen suit — ~$400M court-ordered cleanup (no CWA). The gap-filler where Sackett cuts off CWA wetlands jurisdiction: contamination migrating through soil and groundwater from fill, fuel releases, sludge, or spent treatment chemicals at a campus supports a RCRA citizen suit with injunctive cleanup remedies — no permit violation, no jurisdictional water, and no agency gatekeeping required. How RCRA could apply: Runs parallel to the CWA rather than through it: where a data-center-linked release contaminates groundwater with no surface-water connection, RCRA §7002(a)(1)(B) is the citizen-enforceable federal remedy Sackett left untouched. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp2/263/796/2505473/
- Waiahole-Ditch-2000 (2000) — PTD — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / No CWA action — Hawai'i Supreme Court — trust presumption, burden shift and precautionary principle. The strongest formulation of the trust in American water law, and the direct answer to the evidentiary problem that recurs throughout this dataset. Data center opponents routinely cannot prove harm because consumption figures are confidential and hydrologic effects are contested. Under Waiāhole the applicant carries the burden and uncertainty favours the resource. The caveat is jurisdictional: this rests on Hawai'i's unusually explicit constitutional water provisions, so it marks the doctrine's ceiling rather than a standard other states would apply. How PTD could apply: Persuasive rather than binding outside Hawai'i. Its use is as the argued standard in a state whose own trust doctrine is unsettled: that the data-center applicant, not the objecting public, must justify the draw. Source: http://oaoa.hawaii.gov/jud/21309op.htm
- Trinity-American-v-EPA-SDWA-1431-1998 (1998) — CWA/SDWA — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — SDWA §1431 order upheld — 'contributed to' standard (no CWA). The appellate validation that makes SDWA Section 1431 fast and usable: low causation threshold, no need to wait for completed harm. Land application of nitrate-laden water contaminating rural wells is precisely the Amazon Boardman fact pattern — Trinity American is the case that says EPA could have ordered alternative water there directly. How CWA/SDWA could apply: Where the same land-applied wastewater also reaches surface water via groundwater, County of Maui supplies a parallel CWA §402 theory — the two hooks overlap on exactly the data-center-adjacent fact patterns (Boardman nitrate reuse). Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-4th-circuit/1397077.html
- National-Audubon-v-Superior-Court-1983 (1983) — PTD — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / No CWA action — California Supreme Court — public trust limits appropriative rights. The foundational reopener. Its relevance to data centers is structural: campuses are almost always supplied through an existing municipal or appropriative entitlement rather than a new permit, and the usual assumption is that a settled right is beyond challenge. Audubon says otherwise — the allocation stays reviewable if the resulting draw harms a trust resource, which makes the utility's existing right, not the campus's absent permit, the point of legal leverage. How PTD could apply: Reaches a data center through the *supplier*: a challenge to the utility's or district's existing entitlement on the ground that serving the new load harms a trust resource, rather than a challenge to the campus itself. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/33/419.html
- Sporhase-v-Nebraska-1982 (1982) — EQAP — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — SCOTUS ruling — groundwater is an article of interstate commerce. The constitutional ceiling on state water protectionism, and a live constraint on how the bills in this dataset can be written. A state may limit large withdrawals; it may not condition water on the user or the water staying inside its borders. For data centers this matters because campuses cluster near state lines and draw on shared basins — legislation aimed at keeping water away from a neighbouring state's data center is far more vulnerable than a volume-based cap that applies to everyone. How EQAP could apply: Applies defensively rather than offensively: it is the doctrine under which a data-center operator, or an out-of-state buyer, challenges a state water law that discriminates by destination. Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-supreme-court/458/941.html
- Friendswood-v-Smith-Southwest-1978 (1978) — CL — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — Tex. Supreme Court — negligence exception to the rule of capture for subsidence. The crack in the rule of capture, and the reason a neighbour's strongest claim against a data center in a capture state is about *how* it pumps rather than *that* it pumps. Well spacing, proximity to boundaries and rates chosen against engineering advice are all in scope. It matters most in coastal and alluvial settings where drawdown produces measurable subsidence — which is exactly the Gulf-coast hydrology of the Texas sites tracked here. How CL could apply: A private tort claim by an adjoining landowner against the data center or its water supplier, pleading negligent well siting, spacing or pumping rate rather than the fact of withdrawal. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/texas/supreme-court/1978/b-6682-0.html
- Swanson-v-Marin-MWD-1976 (1976) — UTIL — Landmark Precedent / Water supply & drinking water / No CWA action — Cal. Court of Appeal — no right to new service; moratorium upheld on rational basis. Read in reverse, this is the utility's shield in a data-center fight — and it inverts how these disputes are usually framed. The assumption running through the tracked conflicts is that a utility is under pressure to serve a large new load; Swanson says a utility facing real supply constraint may refuse, and that the would-be customer has no entitlement to be served. Bessemer is the sharp case: the authority conceded on the record that it could not serve 2 MGD without significant upgrades, which is precisely the rational basis a refusal would stand on. How UTIL could apply: Two uses: as the legal basis for a utility or municipality declining to serve a data-center load, and as the standard a developer must meet to overturn such a refusal — fraud, arbitrariness or caprice, not mere disagreement about capacity. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/56/512.html
- Edwards-Aquifer-SoleSource-Designation-1975 (1975) — SDWA — Landmark Precedent / Groundwater & aquifers / No CWA action — SDWA §1424(e) designation — federal-funding review gate (no CWA). The sleeping federal hook for aquifer-country siting: it reaches projects only through federal money, but any federally backed loan, grant, or infrastructure assistance touching a data-center build-out over a designated aquifer (the Edwards region overlaps the Texas data-center boom; the Avra Basin designation sits under Tucson's) opens an EPA contamination review with funding-denial teeth. How SDWA could apply: Complementary rather than alternative to the CWA: §1424(e) reviews the funding of a project over an aquifer, while §404/§402 reach its construction and discharges. Federally financed AI-infrastructure programs would bring this reading into play for aquifer-sited campuses. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/part/149
- US-v-Republic-Steel-RHA-1960 (1960) — RHA — Landmark Precedent / Industrial discharge (§402) / No CWA action — RHA §§10/13 — SCOTUS injunction against industrial deposits (pre-CWA). Two lessons for the data-center era: courts will read old water statutes expansively against new industrial fact patterns, and Corps jurisdiction over structures and obstructions in navigable waters (Section 10) — untouched by Sackett — independently reaches cooling intakes, outfall structures, and river crossings that hyperscale campuses and their power plants are now proposing. How RHA could apply: The CWA §402 permit program replaced Refuse Act prosecutions for discharges, but RHA §10 survives independently: any data-center intake or outfall structure in a traditionally navigable water still needs Corps §10 authorization on top of NPDES — a Sackett-proof second permit gate. Source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/362/482/
- Winters-v-United-States-1908 (1908) — TRIBAL — Landmark Precedent / Citizen suits & court doctrine / No CWA action — SCOTUS — water impliedly reserved with the reservation, senior to later state rights. The oldest doctrine in this registry and, in the arid West, often the most consequential — because it operates on priority rather than on conduct. A data center never has to do anything wrong for this to matter: quantifying a senior reserved right shrinks the pool the state had been allocating, and junior users are cut in order of seniority. A campus whose supply contract rests on a junior state-law right in a basin serving a reservation holds something worth less than its face value, and that is a due-diligence question rather than a litigation risk. How TRIBAL could apply: Reaches a data center indirectly and structurally: not as a claim against the operator, but as a senior right that reduces what the state can allocate to it, in any basin serving a federal reservation. Source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/207/564/

## Data-center sites with documented water conflicts

- google-the-dalles-or — Google — The Dalles, OR (The Dalles, Wasco County, Oregon): Google's water use nearly tripled in five years to over a quarter of everything the city supplies (later reporting puts it near 40%). When The Oregonian requested the numbers in 2021, the city — with Google paying its legal fees — sued the newspaper to keep them secret as a 'trade secret.' Status: Resolved — data disclosed; the case is now the template other communities cite when operators claim water use is confidential. Applicable readings: sdwa-pws-compliance, cwa-307-pretreatment. Source: https://www.rcfp.org/dalles-google-oregonian-settlement/
- xai-colossus-memphis-tn — xAI Colossus — Memphis, TN (South Memphis, Tennessee (former Electrolux site)): Colossus draws roughly 3 MGD of cooling water while the Memphis Sand aquifer — the region's sole drinking-water source — is already being pumped faster than it recharges. xAI promised an $80M recycling plant treating up to ~13 MGD of municipal wastewater to offset withdrawals, then put it on indefinite pause in April 2026 to prioritize Colossus 2. Status: Operating on aquifer-sourced water; recycling plant paused with a promised Q1 2027 restart. Applicable readings: cwa-402-npdes, cwa-307-pretreatment, sdwa-source-water-protection. Source: https://dailymemphian.com/section/metro/article/61680/xai-water-recycling-plant-in-question
- meta-newton-county-ga — Meta — Newton County / Mansfield, GA (Social Circle / Mansfield area, Newton County, Georgia): After Meta broke ground on its $750M campus, nearby well-dependent households — the closest about 1,000 feet away — reported taps running dry, sediment, and pressure loss. The facility uses ~500,000 gal/day (~10% of county water use), and Mansfield's mayor cited 33% water-rate increases over two years. Meta's commissioned study called its impact 'unlikely.' Status: Ongoing dispute; no formal enforcement yet. Applicable readings: sdwa-1431-emergency, sdwa-source-water-protection, cwa-402-construction-stormwater. Source: https://www.sanjuandailystar.com/post/their-water-taps-ran-dry-when-meta-built-next-door
- project-blue-tucson-az — Project Blue — Tucson / Pima County, AZ (Tucson / Pima County, Arizona): The first two sites would have needed ~2,000 acre-feet of water per year — making the campus Tucson Water's largest customer — negotiated under NDAs that kept the end user secret. The city council rejected annexation 7-0 on August 6, 2025 after intense community pressure. Status: City rejection stands; redesigned county-land project proceeding without city water. Applicable readings: sdwa-pws-compliance, sdwa-1424e-sole-source-aquifer. Source: https://azluminaria.org/2025/08/06/tucson-city-council-rejects-project-blue-amid-intense-community-pressure/
- meta-mesa-microsoft-goodyear-az — Meta (Mesa) & Microsoft (Goodyear) — Phoenix metro, AZ (Mesa and Goodyear, Maricopa County, Arizona): Roughly 91 data centers operate in metro Phoenix amid a potential 77% cut to Arizona's Colorado River allocation. Meta's Mesa water agreement allows up to ~4 MGD at full build (with a pledge not to use Colorado River water and to transfer storage credits once demand exceeds 500,000 gal/day); Microsoft's Goodyear campus draws substantial potable water daily. Status: Both operating and expanding under negotiated water commitments. Applicable readings: sdwa-pws-compliance, sdwa-source-water-protection. Source: https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/huge-data-center-moves-forward-in-mesa-despite-arizona-water-concerns/
- pw-digital-gateway-va — PW Digital Gateway — Prince William County, VA (Pageland Lane corridor, Prince William County, Virginia — Occoquan Reservoir headwaters): A 2,100+ acre, up-to-23M sq ft, 37-building rezoning was approved in December 2023 over objections from Fairfax Water and downstream supervisors: the corridor drains to the Occoquan Reservoir, which supplies roughly 40% of Northern Virginia's drinking water (800,000+ people), and the county declined to wait for a water-quality study. Status: Halted — rezonings voided; project dead absent a restart. Applicable readings: sdwa-source-water-protection, cwa-402-construction-stormwater, cwa-404-dredge-fill, cwa-303-wqs. Source: https://www.pecva.org/region/regional-state-national-region/prince-william/massive-digital-gateway-data-center-project-has-been-halted/
- aws-lake-anna-va — AWS Lake Anna Technology Campus — Louisa County, VA (Louisa County, Virginia — Sedges Creek, Lake Anna tributary): A draft VPDES individual permit would let AWS discharge up to 280,000 gal/day of treated cooling water into Sedges Creek — the first direct-to-surface-water hyperscaler cooling-discharge permit in Virginia. Residents packed a March 2026 hearing, and a June 9, 2026 DEQ meeting turned contentious over chemical additives and the draft's lack of required PFAS testing (DEQ kept only a reopener condition). Status: DEQ finalizing its decision after the June hearing; permit not yet issued as of early July 2026. Applicable readings: cwa-402-npdes, cwa-316-cooling, cwa-303-wqs, rha-10-structures, tsca-8a7-pfas-reporting. Source: https://www.12onyourside.com/2026/06/10/deq-meeting-about-data-center-water-discharging-into-lake-anna-tributaries-turns-contentious/
- amazon-boardman-umatilla-or — Amazon/AWS — Boardman & Umatilla, OR (Port of Morrow) (Morrow and Umatilla counties, Oregon — Lower Umatilla Basin): Nitrate-laden Port of Morrow wastewater is used for AWS server cooling; evaporation concentrates the nitrates before the water is land-applied to farm fields above an aquifer where the state has found 634+ domestic wells with unsafe nitrate levels. Residents sued 17 defendants in February 2024. Status: Settlement announced March 31, 2026; underlying reuse-and-land-application system still operating. Applicable readings: sdwa-1431-emergency, rcra-7002-7003-endangerment, cwa-402-maui-groundwater, cwa-307-pretreatment. Source: https://oregoncapitalchronicle.com/2026/03/31/amazon-to-pay-20-5-million-settlement-over-northeast-oregon-nitrate-pollution/
- corpus-christi-sinton-tx — Corpus Christi / Sinton — Evangeline Aquifer, TX (San Patricio County, Texas): With reservoirs below 10% full, Corpus Christi's $650M+, 22-well emergency wellfield in the Evangeline Aquifer near Sinton was protested by the City of Sinton and St. Paul Water Supply Corp.; Corpus officials allege Sinton wants the groundwater to sell to incoming data centers. In May 2026 an administrative law judge let the contested case proceed — a potential multi-year delay. Status: In contested hearings; Corpus continues pipeline spending without drilling permits. Applicable readings: sdwa-source-water-protection, sdwa-pws-compliance. Source: https://insideclimatenews.org/news/19052026/corpus-christi-emergency-water-supply-delays/
- hood-county-granbury-tx — MARA bitcoin mine & proposed AI campuses — Hood County, TX (Granbury, Hood County, Texas — Paluxy Valley watershed): Residents living with the 24/7 roar of MARA's crypto-mine fans (an Earthjustice nuisance suit is ongoing; a 24-foot sound wall failed to help) also raised water-security concerns for the Paluxy watershed as new AI facilities were proposed. Status: No moratorium; nuisance litigation and expansion continue. Applicable readings: sdwa-source-water-protection. Source: https://www.texastribune.org/2026/02/10/texas-hood-county-rejects-data-center-development-pause-ai/
- charlotte-nc-moratorium — Charlotte, NC — citywide data-center moratorium (Charlotte / Mecklenburg County, North Carolina): Amid North Carolina's worst drought since 2007 and voluntary water restrictions, a proposed facility's peak summer demand equal to ~4,000 homes crystallized council concern; a May 2026 hearing drew 36 speakers demanding a pause. Status: Moratorium in force; regulations being drafted. Applicable readings: sdwa-pws-compliance. Source: https://www.wfae.org/politics/2026-06-08/charlotte-city-council-approves-150-day-data-center-moratorium
- microsoft-racine-county-wi — Microsoft — Caledonia & Mount Pleasant, WI (Racine County, Wisconsin (Mount Pleasant/former Foxconn site; abandoned Caledonia parcel)): Microsoft withdrew its Caledonia rezoning in October 2025 after intense resident opposition, while its Mount Pleasant campus — inside the contested Foxconn-era Lake Michigan diversion area under the Great Lakes Compact — expanded through state wetland individual permitting and won approval for 15 more data centers in January 2026. Status: Caledonia dead; Mount Pleasant $4B+ expansion approved with minimal opposition. Applicable readings: cwa-404-dredge-fill, cwa-401-certification, sdwa-pws-compliance. Source: https://www.wpr.org/news/microsoft-caledonia-data-center-site-ozaukee-county
- qts-fayette-county-ga — QTS — Fayetteville / Fayette County, GA (Fayetteville, Fayette County, Georgia — Flint River headwaters): Two high-capacity water connections at the construction campus went unmetered and unbilled — one installed without the utility's knowledge — until the county discovered roughly 29-30 million gallons consumed during drought conditions and retroactively billed QTS $147,474 (the county attributes it to a missed meter reading during a smart-meter transition). Separately, Flint Riverkeeper documented orange flocculant and heavy sediment in headwater creeks below the site after rains. Status: Bill paid and metering fixed; construction-discharge scrutiny continues. Applicable readings: cwa-402-construction-stormwater, cwa-505-citizen-suit, sdwa-pws-compliance. Source: https://thecitizen.com/2026/05/11/behind-fayettes-qts-water-controversy-a-missed-meter-8000-workers-and-a-massive-construction-project/
- meta-richland-parish-la — Meta Hyperion — Richland Parish, LA (Richland Parish (near Rayville/Delhi), Louisiana): State records show Meta's ~$27B, 2+ GW campus is registered for up to 23 MGD of water supply (8.4B gal/yr) — far above Meta's stated expectation of 500-600M gal/yr — under a Louisiana registration regime with no meaningful state monitoring of actual withdrawals. LSU hydrologists warned sustained maximum pumping could harm the aquifer. Status: Under construction, operational target 2028; transparency and cost fights ongoing. Applicable readings: sdwa-source-water-protection, sdwa-pws-compliance, cwa-402-npdes. Source: https://www.nola.com/news/environment/meta-louisiana-data-center-water-ai/article_d27dea17-d571-453c-b5a5-0deb571ea272.html
- quantum-loophole-frederick-md — Quantum Frederick / Q-LOOP — Frederick County, MD (Adamstown, Frederick County, Maryland — Potomac and Monocacy crossings): Boring the 42-mile Q-LOOP fiber conduit under the Potomac and Monocacy produced at least four 'frac-outs' releasing bentonite drilling mud into Potomac-feeding waters. MDE referred the violations to the Maryland Attorney General in September 2023 and in June 2024 rescinded a $130,000 settlement offer, citing the 'ongoing nature and severity' of repeat violations. Status: AG enforcement track operative per latest reporting; campus development continuing under new ownership. Applicable readings: cwa-402-npdes, cwa-404-dredge-fill, rha-10-structures. Source: https://www.bayjournal.com/news/energy/frustrations-mount-with-developer-of-maryland-data-center-complex/article_3af1522a-1d2b-11ef-bbbf-c727c4493083.html
- microsoft-west-des-moines-ia — Microsoft — West Des Moines, IA (West Des Moines, Iowa): The Azure campus that trained GPT-4 used 11.5 million gallons in July 2022 — about 6% of the entire district's water that month — making it one of the first sites where AI training's water intensity was quantified publicly (2023 AP reporting). Microsoft, R&R Realty, and Jordan Creek Town Center are the city's largest water users. Status: Operating; zero-water designs pledged for new buildings. Applicable readings: cwa-307-pretreatment, sdwa-pws-compliance. Source: https://gizmodo.com/microsoft-water-usage-ai-iowa-data-center-1850826419
- bessemer-al-hyperscale — Logistic Land Investments hyperscale campus — Bessemer, AL (Bessemer, Jefferson County, Alabama — Warrior River / Mulberry Fork): The proposed 4.5M sq ft, 18-building campus requested 2 MGD from the Warrior River Water Authority — a third of the authority's ~6 MGD capacity — which said it cannot supply that without 'significant upgrades.' The source (Mulberry Fork of the Black Warrior) is shared with Birmingham-metro supplier Central Alabama Water. Status: Rezoning approved; water-capacity question unresolved ahead of permitting. Applicable readings: sdwa-pws-compliance, cwa-303-wqs, cwa-404-dredge-fill. Source: https://insideclimatenews.org/news/12072025/bessemer-alabama-water-utility-data-center-upgrades/
- missouri-peculiar-stcharles — Missouri municipal backlash — Peculiar & St. Charles, MO (Peculiar (Cass County) and St. Charles, Missouri): Peculiar residents defeated a proposed data center in 2024 over water-rate, traffic, noise, and light concerns — a fight so acrimonious the city administrator and mayor resigned. St. Charles followed in 2025 as one of the first U.S. cities to pass a temporary data-center moratorium, driven partly by water-supply concerns; April 2026 municipal elections statewide showed data centers becoming an electoral liability. Status: Peculiar project dead; St. Charles moratorium era continuing with no state framework. Applicable readings: sdwa-pws-compliance. Source: https://missouriindependent.com/2026/06/05/theyre-already-here-regulating-data-centers-stalls-in-missouri/
